The house in committee on Bill No. 348, for'the relief of Louis Coit Dargavel-Mr. Casselman-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-(Marriage dissolved.

Looking over the evidence in this case, I have come to the conclusion that the bill should not be passed on the evidence which has been presented. There has been no fair trial. The petition is dated February 7, 1929. The charge against the respondent is concerning an offence alleged to have been committed on or about June 1, 1928, at Fayetteville, New York. No attempt was made to prove this charge. No evidence whatever was adduced concerning it. A paid detective was allowed to give evidence concerning other occasions of which the respondent had not the slightest notice and in regard to which she had no opportunity to defend herself.
The respondent was without funds. The insignificant sum of $75 was advanced to her on the order of the committee-a sum totally inadequate to enable her to prepare for trial -and the sum of $75 was advanced to pay counsel-an amount not sufficient to fee a solicitor, much less to pay counsel on the hearing.
The petitioner adduced evidence to show that the respondent and corespondent were registered at a rooming house called Traymore Apartments, in Rochester, N.Y., under the name of " Mr. and Mrs. Rudd." The respondent and corespondent deny this positively on oath, and after a few days' adjournment of -the case the corespondent was able

to produce the man, Guy L. Rudd, who was actually registered at the said apartment house and living there with his wife, and who came before the committee and refuted the evidence o-f petitioner. One of the witnesses who swore that Rudd and wife were the respondent and corespondent recanted and after returning to Rochester made an affidavit that the evidence she had given before the committee was incorrect and that she had never seen the respondent or corespondent until she saw them at the trial before the committee.
The committee refused a further adjournment in order to allow the respondent -to call this recanting witness who admitted that her evidence was untrue, and refused to allow the affidavit to be read before the committee. The corespondent proved that on occasions when the petitioner's witnesses had sworn he was at various places with the respondent he was actually confined to his bed by illness in another town altogether and that it was a physical impossibility for him to have been where the respondent's witnesses swore they saw him. So much of the evidence adduced by the petitioner having been positively shown to be perjury, none of the evidence on behalf of the petitioner is worthy of credence.
The respondent swore-see page 34-that the petitioner proposed that she coftimit the necessary offence upon which to obtain a divorce. This proposal she refused. There was no contradiction of this evidence on her part.
Without doubt further adjournment should have been granted in order to allow the respondent and corespondent to meet the charges that were made against them. In the short time at their disposal they utterly refuted some of the charges and proved the evidence given on behalf of the petitioner to be perjury. Given a reasonable time to check up the other evidence, there is every reason to suppose it also could have been shown to be perjury. Two of these charges were sprung on the respondent and corespondent without notice. They were able entirely to refute all those which could be said to be sufficient ground upon which to grant the petition. As to the remaining occasion, there is not the slightest direct evidence of impropriety. Both the respondent and corespondent gave clear and unequivocal explanation of the circumstances and deny on oath any improper relations either at that time or at any other time.
To grant this divorce on these proceedings would be highly improper. No court of law would permit a case to be presented and tried

Procedure Respecting Divorce
as this one was. In any properly conducted divorce trial, the offence as alleged must be proved. Evidence of offence alleged to have been committed on "divers occasions"-which is the stereotyped language of such petitions- is never allowed by a court except to show the general conduct of the respondent and in a manner as corroboration of the evidence as charged. If the offence as charged is not proved by the evidence no court will grant a divorce.
Where the charge as alleged with particularity, giving place and date, cannot be proved, and petitioner desires to prove other charges, it is the invariable practice to have the petition redrawn alleging definitely the charges it is desired to prove, and to have the petition re-served giving the respondent an opportunity to prepare a defence and to obtain from the petitioner all particulars of the charge.
This primary rule of procedure-to disregard which would be a decided injustice- was altogether ignored by the committee, and neither respondent nor corespondent has had " fr*lr opportunity of making a defence.
This was a contested case, Mr. Chairman, and the evidence is rather bulky. After I had read the evidence I looked back with some anxiety to see whether the divorce committee had really recommended the passing of a divorce bill. It did not seem to me possible that they should do so in view of the fact that Rudd and his wife were not the respondent and the other woman. It c.;ems to me that the case turns very materially on that point, and it strikes me, with all deference to the divorce committee of the Senate-we all recognize that they are human and that everybody makes mistakes, even the courts-that this particular bill should be referred back to the private bills committee for further consideration.

I agree with what has been said by the hon. member. The only charge made in the petition against this respondent was proved to have been a case of perjury. Then other charges were made which were not included in the original petition. As I read the case, no due time was given to the respondent fully to meet those subsequent charges. If a respondent comes before the committee and swears clearly and positively that she has not been guilty of the charge made against her, and, if the original charge as made in the petition is proved to have been founded upon perjury, then any subsequent charges which may be made during the course of that hearing should be made by amendment to the petition, and a re-hearing should be allowed to the respondent in order that she may have opportunity to prove her innocence of these other charges of which she had no previous notice whatsoever before she appeared before the committee.

I am rather surprised that this bill is being opposed in the house. Just a few minutes ago there was placed in my hands the same brief that has just been put on the record by the hon. member for Brant. With many parts of that brief I cannot agree. It would appear to me that when -this matter was before the private bills committee the other day, if any investigation was desired it should have been made at that time, rather than allow the bill to come back here to the committee of the whole house and then ask to have it referred back. I do not wish to suggest that the parties who are opposing this bill are not doing so in good faith, but I think it would have shown better faith on the part of the parties who -are responsible for this action being taken if .they themselves had appeared before the private bills committee.
With regard to the statement that the charge in the petition was not proven, I would suggest that the charges in the original petition covered the offences which were pioven. I have an interest in this case, knowing the parties, and I therefore sat for several days in the committee when this case was being heard. I am perfectly satisfied in my own mind that this applicant had just grounds for divorce. I therefore oppose any move to have the bill sent back to the private bills committee.

In answer to the hon. member, I am not a member of the private bills committee; I have other committees to attend, and in any event I was not -put on that committee and I did not consider it my duty to go there and present any argument. I assumed that the private bills committee would look after their own business. That is all I have to say on that point.

I wish to support the position taken by my hon. friend from Grenville-Dundas. I have read the evidence carefully. I know the parties. The applicant is a resident of the town in which I reside. His wife has not resided with him for a period of fifteen years. This case was contested before the Senate divorce committee, where every opportunity was given to produce evidence, and there was a further opportunity before the private bills committee. It seems

Procedure Respecting Divorce
to me that the position now taken is one of obstruction, at this late date in the session.
I submit that we ought to follow the regular procedure, and as this case has been thoroughly investigated by the Senate committee and in the private bills committee that we ought to adopt their report.

I wish to call attention to
the fact that although these parties had not been living together they had been living separately under a separation agreement since April 17, 1915, and there is a clear suggestion that the object of these divorce proceedings is to allow the husband to escape paying the annuity which he agreed to pay under that separation agreement. In a charge of adultery there should be some time and place mentioned in order that the respondent may be upon her guard and may be able to show where she was, in what company she was, and under what circumstances she was living at the time the alleged adultery took place. In this ease there is only one specific date mentioned, and that is June 1, 1928, and the place mentioned is Fayetteville, in the state of New York, and the charge with respect to the adultery alleged to have been committed on June 1, 1928, at Fayetteville was proved to be utterly false.

Referring to the separation agreement which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has just mentioned, it contains a clause that the payments were to be made only so long as the respondent remained of chaste character. There was that limitation, and there is an exhibit of a letter sent by the respondent to her husband in which she herself offers in consideration of $3,000 to consent to divorce and to produce the evidence that will support the divorce.

As a member of the
private bills committee I wish to say a word in regard to this case. One hon. gentleman has suggested that it is the business of the members of the private bills committee to go into these cases. Personally, I may say that I have neither the time nor the inclination to go into these three hundred divorce cases. This is just another illustration to show what a farce this divorce business is so far as consideration before the private bills committee is concerned. I hope the Prime Minister will implement his promise that next year there will be a different arrangement with . respect to divorce.
As regards the remark that was made by one hon. gentleman that bills that have passed the private bills committee should not be considered in committee of the whole house because the private bills committee should at-

tend to their business, I would ask what is this committee of the whole for? Have we just to give a perfunctory approval to the bills that come from the private bills committee? I say that if any evidence has come out since the private bills committee sat on this case, it is the duty of this committee to consider such evidence and to listen to what may be said.

On section 1-Marriage dissolved.
Explain.

I wish to make a comment
on this bill. On the second reading of the bill the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) went over the evidence, pointing out its weaknesses, and it was assumed by the committee of the whole that when the bill was referred back to the private bills committee special consideration would be given it. As a matter of fact, when the bill did get before that committee no particular attention was given to it. It is time that consideration of the billwas postponed for two days, and the officers of the committee were instructed to inform the respondent when the case would come before the committee. The so-called agents of the respondent were not present; in fact, it happened that the respondent had no official agent, for the lawyer had received no instructions: in other words, the woman had no money and there was no way of going on with the matter. The result was that nothing was done. When the bill came up I endeavoured to present the petition to the committee, but it was another "I'm Alone" case; nobody paid any attention to it. No investigation was made and no evidence seriously presented.
I wish once more to make a plea on behalf of the respondent. First, let me say that I do not know the respondent at all. I would point out that the most material witness in favour of the respondent was unable to give evidence before the senate committee for the reason that she had passed through a very serious operation. There was no doubt about the serious condition of the witness, for there [DOT] was evidence to prove that clearly. Counsel or the lesipondent asked that t'he case be postponed or that an opportunity be given for this material witness to appear. The chairman of the committee in reply said something to the effect that it was very difficult to ensure that the same personnel who had heard the evidence in the first instance would be present on a subsequent occasion, and for that reason a postponement of the case was not granted. The result was that this witness was not heard.
I understand that this witness proposed to prove an alibi; that is to say, at the time and in the places where the illegal acts were sup-78594-220
posed to have been committed it could be proved that the respondent was not present at all, thus substantiating her claim that the case was a frameup. She denies the charge, claiming that there was a frameup, and the most material witness was unable to give evidence.
There is another feature of the case. I believe there are three corespondents mentioned. The respondent, not knowing of course the methods which would be adopted by the petitioner, did not know how many corespondents would be cited and consequently did not have an opportunity to call them. It must be remembered also that this is a poor woman who has been working for her living; she received S75 by order of the committee in order to carry on the case but could not afford to add enough to that sum to pay for her lawyers and to see that the case was properly conducted. Furthermore, if she was advised that our committee was to reconsider this bill-and I do not know whether or not she was so advised-she was working and if she had given uip her work and come down here she might have lost her position.
In view of the circumstances and in view of the fact that the petitioner cannot suffer very much if this bill is left over for another year, I do not see why this committee should not give this woman the benefit of the doubt and kill this bill for the time being; it can be brought up again next year and all these further points considered. That seems a reasonable request, and in view of the fact that perhaps not over two per cent of the members of this' committee know anything about this bill I think it would be a very serious responsibility for us to pass it now.

I also carefully read the
evidence in this case and I am confident that if I were sitting as a judge I would not grant a divorce on the evidence which was presented. Furthermore the respondent, in this case a woman, came before the committee and swore positively as to her innocence, and when it was found impossible to prove the first charge that was made, if I remember correctly an amendment was allowed. Where a respondent comes before a committee and swears positively as to her innocence, in my opinion no new charges should be allowed to be presented against her without an amendment being made to the petition and ample opportunity being given the respondent to bring her witnesses in respect to the new charges. The evidence, to me, is quite consistent with being a frame-up and therefore I think there should be further investigation

Procedure Respecting Divorce
in this case and that the respondent should have a further opportunity to bring a witness who was proved to be ill at the time and present her defence to the amended charge. I intend to vote against this bill.

Fisheries Act Amendment
I may explain, Mr. Chairman, that this bill has been before the committee on marine and fisheries on several occasions, and as now presented1 it is in the form accepted by that committee.

The
committee recommended that trawlers be licensed. Where does that recommendation appear in this bill?
Clause 7.
Another bill is now being handed around. There was an amended bill on the commons bills file which did not contain what is in the bill now being handed to us.

Which
portion of clause 7 deals with the licensing of trawlers?

Clause 7. Let me read it:
7. The said act is further amended by inserting the following section immediately after section sixty-nine thereof:-
69a. (1) Every person shall be guilty of an offence, and shall incur therefor a penalty of not less than one hundred dollars and not more than two thousand dollars, recoverable with costs upon summary conviction, who at any time, except under license from the minister,-.
And the following section indicates in what circumstances a license may be obtained. There is also subsection 4 on page 3:

(a) Prescribing the form of license;

I desire, Mr. Chairman, to offer a few comments on the bill. This bill, I fake it, represents the government's intention in the matter of implementing the findings of a commission appointed to inquire info the difficulties, problems and disabilities of the fishermen of the eastern section of the maritime provinces. It must be a matter of deep regret to those of us who come from fishing communities, as I know it must be to the fishermen themselves, to find that this is the only piece of legislation that the government has to offer in connection with the findings of a commission which has coat this country upwards of $100,000. As a remedy for the deplorable conditions depicted by this commission this bill is practically valueless. There are upwards of seventy recommendations made by the commission. The government had this report in its hands for over a year, and I regret to see that after a year's consideration the only legislation that the government was able to
bring down is this bill, which is entirely innocuous and leaves the situation in exactly the same condition as it was when the commission was appointed. The only difference is that, as the hon. minister has said, the words "licensing of steam trawlers" are inserted in this bill.
Among its many recommendations the commission recommend that the fishermen should be properly organized so that they might be able to get more of the consumer's dollar for their product. They also recommend the etablishment of co-operative organizations to be assisted by the department, and that an organizer be appointed and paid by the federal government for a period of time in order to start the work. This is the crux of the situation and yet the government has done nothing.
The royal fisheries commission states that if the inshore fisheries in the maritimes are to succeed, organization and co-operation are absolutely essential among our fishermen. On page 81 of the report the commission recommends that in certain districts or zones, cooperatives should be formed and supplied with small brine or rapid freezing plants, having small auxiliary cold storage buildings in connection. These should be placed within a days transportation of a larger cold storage plant, the latter having a waste fish product plant in connection. This would take care of the surplus from the smaller plants. They also recommend a marketing sales board to control the output of the product to various sections and that selling agents be appointed in the larger communities to control distribution and protect the market. Equipped with this organized power of bargaining, the fishermen could dictate reasonable prices to the consumer as well as secure a reasonable profit for their labour. Under such a plan long term loans for the purchase of boats, equipment and also insurance of fishermen's property could be arranged through the fishermen's organization. The royal commiasion believes that these suggestions would solve the fishermen's problems, and would establish a profitable industry and secure for him an assured market and a bargaining power which he has not thus far possessed, and a greater portion of the consumer's dollar than he has hitherto received.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as far as I can see, those recommendations have not been carried out. As regards section 5 of the old bill, I take the stand taken by the fishermen in the eastern section of Nova Scotia, that the beam trawler is to a large extent responsible for the condition that now exists in our maritime
Fisheries Act Amendment

province fisheries, and I claim it is the duty of this government to accept the majority report of that commission if they are going to do anything for the fishermen of the maritime provinces.
I am unalterably opposed to the beam trawler fish landing in Canada, and I ask this government what it has done to protect our north Atlantic fishing grounds from the depredations of the foreign trawler. The fisheries report has asked for a conference of the nations concerned in reference to this destructive method of fishing. Thus far nothing has been done. Mr. Chairman, I claim that the use of the beam trawler is one of the most destructive methods that could be devised; firstly, for the reason that large quantities of immature and inedible fish are caught through this method and are destroyed. These fish are either thrown overboard dead, or taken to a fish meal plant for reduction and placed on the market as fish meal or fertilizer. Secondly, the beam trawler destroys the spawning fish, thus seriously interfering with fish propagation. Dr. W. L. Fulton, superintendent of scientific investigation in Scotland, claims that thirty per cent of the trawler catch consists of immature inedible fish. The spawning fish taken by the beam trawlers on our banks are not taken to any extent by the methods employed by the inshore fishermen, as sick fish spawning will not readily take the hook and line. I submit that means should be taken to restrict the trawler method if we are going to conserve our fisheries in the maritime provinces, and especially our north Atlantic coast fisheries. Thirdly, the beam trawler net with its iron shod doors drags the bottom of the sea and disturbs and destroys the algae and the fungi on which the fish depend for food.
My contentions are borne out by the fact that in the North sea fishing grounds off the coast of England where beam trawling originated, the fish catch is decreasing year by year on account of the employment of the trawler method. Where formerly they fished an area of 152,000 square miles, they are now compelled to extend over an area of over 700,000 square miles, and are not supplying an amount equal to that of former years.
Spain, Portugal, France and English beam trawlers are to-day compelled to come to our north Atlantic waters and fish on our banks, by reason of the depletion of their own fishing grounds. The United States consuming public are becoming disturbed over the depletion of haddock in the north Atlantic and are today advocating a conference between Canada, the United States and all nations operating beam trawlers in order to arrive at ways and means whereby this most valuable fresh fish
 *
product may be conserved. The beam trawler method of fishing gives to the consuming public an inferior product. Fish are by far the most perishable of all foodstuffs and if they are not frozen by the rapid freezing, or what is sometimes known as the brine freezing, method as soon as they are taken from the sea, they lose their texture, that is they become soft; they lose their flavour and also become a prey to bacteria, resulting in rapid deterioration, giving rise to ptomaine poisoning.
The fish taken by the beam trawler are injured by their own weight and by the foreign material taken into the trap. The lower portion of the catch are bruised and crushed by the great mass of material in the trap before they reach the deck of the trawler. This fish is placed in bulk in the hold of the ship or in pens or on shelves and there iced, and the melting ice pours down on the fish below, further softening it, and carrying with it products of bacterial decomposition. The greater part of this fish is kept from five to nine days sometimes longer before being landed. This fish is then placed in cold storage to be frozen by the slow method. Depending upon the amount landed by each trawler, some 200,000 to 300,000 pounds, this requires some two or three days. The fish is then held in storage for three to six months before being placed on the market for human consumption. The product is much inferior to our inshore catch, which is generally marketed the day it is caught. The inshore fish retains its texture, its flavour, and is a very much superior product. The condition in which the beam trawder fish reaches the consumer is the reason it is so difficult to retain the market of central Canada.
In my opinion the greatest objection by inshore fishermen to the beam trawler method is the glutting of the market by over production, giving to the inshore fisherman a very restricted market and consequent low prices -prices which will not permit of an adequate livelihood. Our shore fisherman is thus compelled to give up his occupation, close his home, move to the United States and engage in the American fishing industry, which to-day gives him a livelihood denied to him in his own country. Since 1912, ten thousand fishermen have left the maritime provinces. In one school section alone thirty-three children left with their parents and moved to the United States in a little over three months, and in March, 1929, practically five hundred fishermen left the small section of Isle Madame for the United States to engage in the American fishing industry. Some two hundred have left the river Bourgeois section of Richmond county during the past

Fisheries Act Amendment
two months. The result is that the New England fisheries are to-day almost entirely manned by Nova Scotians. Would it not be a better policy to try to do something for our own fishing industry and retain our native sons instead of spending $20,000,000 as we have done in eight years to bring aliens into Canada?
The mass beam trawler production of which I have spoken has driven our inshoreman from his customary rights,, rights which have been his from time immemorial. Our inshore fisheries have played the most important part in the colonization and development of the maritimes. The thriving, happy and contented fishing villages of earlier days are now a thing of the past, and in their places are to be found ruined fishing establishments, boats and gear decaying, homes closed, their former occupants to-day in a foreign land, lost to this country forever.
The problem to-day is a choice between the dividends paid to a group of capitalists who are operating a destructive method of fishing, producing an inferior article, employing some two hundred and forty-nine men, with an invested capital of $990,000, and the livelihood of sixteen thousand fishermen, with an invested capital of $24,000,000. One or the other must go, and it is up to this government to protect the interests of our native born inshore fishermen.
Would the sixteen thousand fishermen my hon. friend refers to be shore fishermen only? There are some forty thousand altogether.

That is, in Canada. The friends of the beam trawler claim that the inshore fishermen cannot supply the demand. That is their only claim, and I would ask the minister whether this government has ever given the inshore fishermen of the province of Nova Scotia an opportunity to try to supply the demand for fresh fish. The government has not done so. In 1928 the inshore fishermen of Nova Scotia furnished about one half of the fresh fish marketed by our various corporations, and they have also sent to foreign markets, in its dried and salted state, almost double the quantity supplied by the beam trawlers. The fishermen in that province have not been given an opportunity, and under this legislation-although we have spent $100,000-we are receiving no consideration. I regret that, in spite of the conditions which have been described by the royal commission, this government has treated the situation in the way it has done.

With much that my hon. friend has just said I must agree, though not with all. The condition of the fishermen in the maritime provinces is a great blot on the economic life of Canada to-day; there is no other class of the com-munitiy I know of which is in such a pauperized state. I have not lived in that country long enough to know just what has brought this about, but I had the opportunity of going down there twice in recent years.
And caught a salmon.

Thank you;
I was fortunate enough to do that. The hon. gentleman is not a fisherman, I take it, or he would enjoy with me the thrill I had in catching it.

It 'was the first you
caught.

No; I had caught several on the Pacific coast before that. I found that in some districts many of the fishermen were wholly illiterate. Even to-day some families are growing up without education. The average fisherman, in Cape Breton at least, is fortunate if he has an income of $500 in the year. I wish hon. gentlemen would just try to fix their annual budget on the basis of $500 a year. These men, for years, for generations, have lived by such a low standard that their intelligence and aggressiveness have poured out of that country into other countries or into other parts of Canada, or have been completely sup. pressed by the economic conditions under which they exist. I see now, however, a ray of hope in the fact that they are at last beginning to think cooperatively, and if the government could find any means whatever of helping to ignite that little spark that has just started they would have performed splendid service.
Travelling up the west coast of Cape Breton you will find at the north end of one shore the old Scottish Hectorians, if I may use that term, the descendants of the first Scottish people who came to Canada. These people have not only retained their original facial appearance and general physical structure, but even their tongue is as pure to-day as when they came here. I was a little alarmed on one occasion in this house, Mr. Chairman, when a barbaric sound broke out from immediately to your left; but after visiting Cape Breton I find that these hon. gentlemen who on that occasion started some Gaelic songs were simply carrying out the
Fisheries Act Amendment
I would like to ask my hon. friend a question. Do I understand that he is in favour of the majority recommendation of the royal commission with regard to the abolition of beam trawlers?

Sentimentally, yes, but as a practical proposition I do not see how you are going to abolish a trawler which is international in character. That is the difficulty I see; you have beam trawlers coming from all parts of the world, from France, from Portugal, from Spain, from England, from Norway and from the United States, and it seems to me it would be a very stupid thing to destroy Canadian trawler fishing unless it were done by international agreement, and so apply to the trawlers of all nations. I think there should be a limitation, and you should try to build up the morale of the shore fishermen and give them more confidence in their future. You should do what you can to help them market their fish at a better price.
Get them trawlers.

The way to help them get trawlers is to assist them in organizing first and then lend them the money, taking security on the trawler itself. I believe the trawlers cost from $135,000 to $150,000; that is not a very large sum of money, although it must appear a tremendous sum to the shore fishermen. To a government it is a mere bagatelle which is chucked away here and there several times in the course of one day when we are passing estimates sometimes without even decent consideration. If you can only get the fishermen to organize

Fisheries Act Amendment

they will be quite willing to undertake the responsibility in these matters if they see an opportunity of ever getting their heads above the economic slough in which they are immersed at present. Frankly, I would hesitate to picture to the house conditions down there, as I saw them. They were deplorable. I went into one home where there were five children, the eldest of whom was a girl of seventeen, very polite and very pretty. I had heard that she had never been to school, but I wanted to find out for myself, and when I asked her she told me that that was the case because her mother had to go to work in order to make fifty or seventy-five cents per day to keep the home going, and so the girl was required to look after the other four children. The next child was a boy of eleven years of age, and when I asked him if he had ever been to school, he told me that he had not because his father was getting along in years and required his services in the boat in order to steady it while he set the lines for fishing. It is necessary that these boats go out from five to ten miles from the shore, depending on the condition of the weather and the fish, and someone is needed to steady the boat and the sons, and in many cases the daughters of the fishermen, are taken along to do this work because the fathers cannot afford to hire any help; the result is that we have in Canada in the year 1929 a condition of illiteracy which is a disgrace to the country. This is brought about as a result of economic conditions which the minister -would be well advised to look into to see if this question cannot be solved in some way.
I must say quite frankly that I am puzzled as regards the trawlers. If I thought it would save the lives of ten or twenty thousand fishermen and keep them in Canada and build up their business, and if I thought it would not damage the Canadian fishing industry, I would be in favour of abolishing the trawler, but I am in doubt as to just what the effect would be. In Great Britain and other places where the trawler has been used for many years the fishing has become almost non-existent, or at least it has been very largely destroyed. Any hon. member who comes from that part of the world knows that that is the case. Reference was made to agricultural machinery and it was said that it would be just as foolish to prevent the use of the binder as it would be to prevent the use of the trawl, but that is not a fair comparison to make, the binder does not destroy the land, nor does it destroy the grain, and it has been stated on fairly accurate authority 
that the trawler does both; it destroys the fishing beds and destroys a lot of immature fish. On the other hand, other authorities state that that is not the ease, so I find it impossible to arrive at an intelligent answer to this question. 1 think the minister should take the whole matter into consideration and give it his personal attention, as the conditions which prevail in that part of the country are not a credit either to his department or to the Dominion of Canada.

During the recess, would the minister be good enough to secure the file in connection with the Ellis royal commission. The report was tabled a short time ago, but one of our members is very desirous of having this report.
The report has been tabled.

But not the file connected with it. There are some matters antecedent to the report which some members are very anxious to inquire into, as it affects their ridings.

On section 3-Minister may cancel license.

A number of licenses are issued by the minister under the provisions of chapter 73 of the revised statutes. For instance, under section 9 of that statute there is a license in respect of whale fishing; in the same section there is a license for whaling in Hudson bay and northern waters. Under section 10 there is a license for manufacturing fish meal; under section 20, a license in British Columbia waters for boats and buyers of fresh salmon; under section 22, a license in British Columbia for the herwing fishing; under section 23, a license for lobster canning or curing; under section 28, a license for lobster pounds, and so forth. Again I am not suggesting any Amendment expressing want of confidence in the minister, but the proposed new section 8A provides:
The minister may cancel any license issued under the authority of this act, if the operations under such license are not conducted in conformity with law'.
That leaves the cancellation as a mere exercise of discretion on the part of the minister. It does not provide for any evidence

Fisheries Act Amendment
being presented to the minister of any violation of this statute. I suggest that, in case of its being alleged that any holder of a license has not acted in conformity with the law, ae should have an opportunity to be heard and to present evidence in support of his innocense of any such alleged violation. These iicenses are held in many cases by persons and companies who have invested many thousands and sometimes tens of thousands of dollars in the particular fishery for which they have obtained a license, and it seems a hardship that their licenses should be cancelled without an opportunity being given them to be heard. Therefore I move this amendment:
That section 3 be amended by inserting be-ween the words "if" and "the" in the seventeenth line the following words:
"It has been ascertained by the report of a commissioner appointed under the provisions of the Inquiries Act, chapter 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, that"
The clause as amended will then read as follows:
8A. The minister may cancel any license issued under the authority of this act, if it has been ascertained by the report of a commissioner appointed under the provisions of the Inquiries Act, chapter- 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, that the operations under such license are not conducted in conformity with law.
We are now laying down the law for future time with regard to such cancellations, and this amendment provides simply that the licensee, in case a charge is made against him, may be heard under the Inquiries Act. I would be willing to adopt any other method of inquiry that might seem more suitable, but this is the form of inquiry which we have provided for by statute. I have shown my amendment to the minister and I trust that, after due consideration, he will be prepared to accept it.

My hon. friend was kind enough to communicate to me the amendment he proposed to make to this section of the bill. After looking into the matter, I am quite agreeable to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend and to incorporate his amendment in the section.
I think this amendment should be considered a little. I should like to ask the minister if the licenses referred to include licenses granted to lobster and other fishermen under the Fisheries Act?
All licenses.

My hon. friend who moved the amendment should take into consideration the fact that when we issue
licenses to lobster fishermen, it is simply a matter of regulating the fishing and seeing that they obey the law. One of the most objectionable features in connection with that fishery is the difficulty of getting the fisherman to leave the spawn lobsters in the water. We give him a license and if he is found to disobey that regulation, which is important to the industry, his license is cancelled. That is the only control that we have over him. You could not get a commissioner under Inquiries Act to investigate a case of that kind.
Why not.

Are you going
to send him out on the water to watch the men? That is impossible. If the department is satisfied from the evidence that the fishermen is not acting in conformity with the law, then the word of the inspector or police officer or whoever is enforcing the act should be sufficient to have the license cancelled.

How do you manage it
now?

It is now in
the hands of the department.
What do they know about the evidence against him?
They have the word of the officer who is enforcing the law.
Would not the commissioner have that?
The commissioner could only investigate the case afterwards. I think the amendment is entirely unworkable from a practical standpoint.

There is no reason why you could not appoint the officer who is enforcing the law as a commissioner to investigate the case. It is certainly not an objection that the commissioner cannot be on board one of these boats because the fishery inspector is not on the boat either when it is on the water, and he must decide on hearsay or other evidence of some sort.

Evidence, but
not hearsay. A commissioner under the Inquiries Act would not decide on hearsay.

Of course not, and I wish to avoid the possibility that any partisan or any person who is personally hostile to this particular fisherman can merely by writing a letter secure the cancellation of his license. In some cases these men have thousands of dollars invested and the cancellation of the

Fisheries Act Amendment
license destroys the entire property value. Therefore, there should be some method whereby, before the license is cancelled, the particular licensee complained of should have the opportunity to be heard on oath or to present the evidence of his witnesses on oath. That is what I aim suggesting. I quite agree with the hon. member that if the fishermen do not conform to the law their licenses should be cancelled, but the cancellation of the license should depend upon an inquiry at which those who are opposed to its cancellation may have the opportunity to be heard; and the minister should have a (report from the person who conducts that inquiry on oath, upon which in the exercise of his full discretion he may cancel the license. I aim not proposing to take away .the discretion of the minister to ,cancel.	I am simply providing
that he should have evidence on both sides, if available, before such cancellation takes place.

I have heard of no complaints from the fishermen or from the officers enforcing the law with regard to trouble in getting information. I think the law is being administered fairly to both, but the amendment of my hon. Mend would set up too much machinery and there would be too much expense connected with it. You might as well take away the license to fishermen altogether, so far as preserving the industry is concerned, if you enact such an amendment into law.

I cannot possibly understand that, because under the law as it is at present this license may be cancelled by order of the governor in council, and it is proposed now to vest the sole discretion in the minister.
As it is now.
No, as proposed by this amendment.
As it always has been.

Not so. Under the law, as it stood before, the minister had molt that discretion. In exercising his discretion the minister was acting under an order of the governor in council authorizing it, and the governor in council assumed full responsibility for every such cancellation.
It would be cancelled upon the recommendation of the minister of the department.

Quite so, but there was full governmental responsibility in the exercise if that power of cancellation. I am simply 
trying to ensure that those who hold licenses shall not have their licenses cancelled without being heard in their own defence as to whether they have violated the law or not. We are now enlarging the act so that it refers not only to lobster fishing. The old act refers to whale fisheries and a great number of fisheries conducted by large undertakings, and we are how making the act apply to licences for trawling and tihe like, under which business is done in a large way. I think there should be opportunity given to these people to be heard, before their licenses are cancelled. That is my suggestion.

Rather than see the amendment pass in the form suggested by my hon. friend I think it would be better to drop the section altogether. I can see the point he makes as regards the large vested interests being injured if licenses are cancelled, but the member for Queens and myself have in mind the operation of the law as it applies to the fisherman's license, the one dollar license. Out in British Columbia the Japs get a license and they farm it out. They get a license in their own name and sell it to somebody else; it may be to someone in a remote fishing place,, and if we have to put into operation the clauses of the Inquiries Act before we can take that license away, the fishing season will be over. The amendment would also involve an enormous expense because there would have to be advertising, and notice given of the time and place where a meeting was to be held. It would be of no use whatever in protecting the individual fisherman, and would be a great burden on the department in administering the law. No one has ever heard of anyone having been unjustly treated, and I really think it would be better to drop the section then to accept the amendment.

I think the amendment may at first give rise to some suspicion, but I believe it is workable. There is no objection to it that I or the deputy minister can at present see, and no objection to our fishery officers being appointed commissioners to make these investigations. I think that can be easily done under the law.

Is the decision left to the
minister after the evidence is taken?
Absolutely.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 4 and 5 agreed to.

On section 6-publication.

Under the law as it now
stands and under the proposed amendment the regulations go into effect on being published in the Canada Gazette. In addition to that, under the statute as it now stands, these regulations are subsequently published with the volume of statutes for the year. Nearly every country justice of the peace has access to the statutes of Canada as published from year to year, and it gives greater publicity I think to these regulations if the statutes for the year can be examined, as they are now examined, to ascertain the purport of the regulations made from time to time. The sole difference is the very slight cost of publishing these regulations with the annual statutes. The regulations come into full force and effect immediately upon publication in the Canada Gazette, but at present in order to give greater publicity they are also published in the appendix to the statutes for the year. Throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion few people have access to the Canada Gazette; but in almost every country village they have access to the annual statutes and the information contained therein as to such regulations.

This amendment has been
suggested to us by the Justice department. Their contention is that the publication of these regulations in the appendix to the yearly statutes has on many occasions unnecessarily delayed their publication. So we have decided to act on that recommendation.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Penalty for using trawls, etc.

Subsection 2 provides:
No such vessel shall carry on fishing operations from or to any Canadian port or ports, unless such vessel is registered as a British ship in Canada.
I move that subsection 2 of section 7 be amended by adding after the word "is" in the third line the words "built and." The subsection will then read:
No such vessel shall carry on fishing operations from or to any Canadian port or ports, unless such vessel is built and registered as a British ship in Canada.
I move this amendment because of the fact that for years criticisms have been made in this house and elsewhere that our shipbuilding plants have been allowed to remain idle. When the government was building the merchant marine ships several tenders were let to the Halifax Shipyards and other shipbuilding plants throughout the Dominion, and the
ships they turned out, were equal to any built in any other part of the world. I was very much surprised When tenders were let to British concerns for the ships for the West Indies service. The reason given was that they could be built so much cheaper on the other side of the Atlantic. I do not consider that a sufficient reason. We have been spending millions of dollars on immigration and colonization, and this expenditure has been criticized on many occasions on the ground that facilities were not granted to our people to produce what they consume and use. Here is one means of helping to solve our immigration problem. If we want ships for our mercantile marine, let them be built in Canada, and so give our workmen an opportunity to demonstrate what they can do. We ought to make ourselves as far as possible a self-contained nation. Let us give every advantage to the Canadian producer; that is real protection. Let us enable our Canadian workmen to demonstrate their ability to build fishing trawlers, instead of giving advantages to workmen abroad.

Although I am in sympathy with the policy advocated by my hon. friend from Halifax in regard to encouraging our shipbuilding industry, I cannot accept his amendment. It would have the effect of practically confiscating a certain number of vesesls which are now in operation and have been for a period of years. We are not losing the benefit of that operation, because most of these vessels are fishing from Halifax. As to the future, the recommendation of the committee on marine and fisheries, which we are accepting by this bill, provides a remedy. If my hon. friend will refer to paragraph (c) of subsection 5 of section 7, he will see that regulations may be adopted to fix the conditions under which a license shall be issued. Then we may make any other provision respecting licenses. So that in so far as the future is concerned, the bill empowers the minister to meet the situation suggested by my hon. friend. I submit, however, that it would be most unfair at the present time to provide that no licenses shall be issued to an existing trawler on the ground that it was not built in Canada. I hope my hon. friend realizes the position in which his amendment would place us; it would bring about an injustice. I would ask him, therefore, to withdraw it, assuring him that the views he has expressed with respect to encouraging shipbuilding in Canada are shared absolutely by the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Fisheries Act Amendment

I have listened carefully to
what the minister has said and I wish to impress upon him my motive in proposing this amendment. We have been studying, year after year, the problem of maintaining our Canadian citizenship, and how best to meet the immigration question. I have looked over this bill carefully and have come to the conclusion that the amendment I suggest is one way of making a beginning. The firms that are operating trawlers out of Nova Scotia have done more for the shore fishermen than any of the other firms that are carrying on the fish business there, because they have created throughout the country a market for their fish. They would not be operating trawlers out of Nova Scotia ports to-day if they were able to get a regular supply from the shore fishermen. As everyone knows, there are seasons of the year when the shore fishermen do not operate. We do not have any fish on the shore during the winter months, and that is when there is the greatest demand for fish throughout the country. The maritime provinces had no fresh fish market until we were able to give the cities of the upper provinces a regular supply of fish every week. The concerns that are operating the steam trawlers would not be operating one of them if they could get a sufficient quantity of fish from the boat fishermen because it is a well-known fact that the fish landed by the boat fishermen are of a better quality than that landed by the trawlers, but during the winter months it is impossible to get a regular supply of fish from the boat fishermen along our shores in Nova Scotia, and we have to use modern methods in order to ensure a regular supply. knows that the fisheries committee has not recommended their total abolition, but has realized that regulation is necessary. He knows that such a good friend of the fishermen of Nova Scotia as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) who spoke this morning, does not advocate the total abolition of the trawlers. My hon. friend has endeavoured to play on words, but as yet he has made no declaration of his own in regard to this very important matter.
Oh yes.

He says the responsibility is on the government. Well, the government is taking the responsibility of bringing down this legislation. My hon. friend speaks of this bill being brought down in the "dying hours" of the session. It was first introduced on February 14, 1929. I was not a member of that committee, but my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Macdonald) was, and he knows what occurred in the committee. The committee's recommendation is being dealt with by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries within a week after it was submitted to the house. So my hon. friend can find no fault with the government for delay in the matter. This talk about the dying hours of the session is simply an endeavour to draw a red herring across the trail, and to give him an opportunity for making a speech -something that my hon. friend can do very cleverly indeed-to give the fishermen the idea that he is in sympathy with them-
My hon. friend does not seriously wish to say-
Order.

-but failing absolutely
to make any concrete or practical suggestion for helping in the solution of a problem which, as I say. has baffled our people for the last seventeen or eighteen years. This legislation is an endeavour to arrive at a solution of the problem. It will enable the people interested to make representations, and afford the minister an opportunity to weigh those representations and to lay down some principle which will be of benefit to the industry. And when I speak of the "industry" I do not mean the trawlers, I do not mean the companies, I do not mean the corporations; I mean the men and women who day by day are engaged in earning their livelihood in this occupation.

I think, Mr. Chairman, this question should be considered very calmly and coolly. There is no question of doubt that the problems surrounding the fishing industry of Nova Scotia are of a very

acute character. But how any person in these modem times could conceive of abolishing absolutely the trawler-the instrument that has made the Nova Scotia fishing industry broaden out in the Dominion-is more than I can understand. It would be like the western country abandoning the gang plough in favour of the one furrow plough, or our textile manufacturers reverting to the spinning-wheel. It is regrettable that certain fishing districts in Nova Scotia are to' some extent suffering on account of the operations of the steam trawler, but if the steam trawler were completely abolished the province generally would suffer. Take the coal industry, for instance, approximately $100,000 worth of coal is sold to steam trawlers annually, and that coal is mined in Nova Scotia and these trawlers are also provisioned in Nova Scotia. Therefore I think we should approach the discussion of this question not provincially or parochially but on the basis of a broad national question. Our fishing industry as it is now being developed finds an expanding market all over the Dominion.
It has been said that the fishing corporations are making excessive profits. I am told they are not. An hon. member of this house, thoroughly conversant with the fishing industry and also following that business, claims that they have not made anything like excessive profits in the past four or five years. This question should be considered and debated in a calm, sensible way in the light of modern science and advancement in all our industrial pursuits, including fishing. The steam trawlers do not operate within twelve miles of the coastline of Nova Scotia.
What is the good of the bill?

I am merely discussing the question of the steam trawler, which seems to be the paramount issue before the house at the present moment. The hon. member for Bow River stated this morning that the steam trawler had disastrous effects on the fishing industry off the Orkneys in the old country. The royal commission appointed by this government to investigate and study the fisheries in the maritime provinces held, both in the minority and in the majority report, that the operations of the steam trawler have not had a disastrous effect on the fishing industry of the maritime provinces.
I do not think we should have any desire to cripple an industry which is developing and making considerable headway in Canada. We have had sufficient evidences of coopera-

Fisheries Act Amendment
tion with regard to the marketing of our products; I need refer only to the Maritime Provinces Association in the city of Toronto and another one in the city of Montreal, both endeavouring to assist us in the marketing of maritime products in central Canada. If, therefore, we should make any move which would cripple an industry of such importance and with such far-reaching ramifications as the fishing industry, it would simply be tying the hands of those who are willing to assist us, who have been assisting us, and who in the future will give us more in the way of assistance than we can do for ourselves so far as finding outside markets for maritime provinces products including fish.

Mr. Chairman, before the
vote is taken on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn), I wish to give the reason for the vote I am about to cast. The hon. member moved an amendment to Bill No. 26, an amendment which bears on the Fisheries Act, that a clause be inserted in the act so as to provide that licenses be refused to owners of vessels unless such vessels are built in Canada, and the reason given by the hon. member for Halifax in support of this amendment was that he wants the workers interested in the building of vessels to be employed. In my opinion, the hon. member for Halifax could have found a more appropriate circumstance to help these workers. He told us a short while ago that we could in Canada, as well as anywhere else, build vessels as sound and as cheap as those built by English firms. This is not so. On every occasion that the Canadian government requested our ship-builders and those of English firms to submit tenders, Canadian firms had to ask 30 per cent more than the English firms, and- the contracts which, under these circumstances, were awarded to Canadian builders, brought ruin upon them. Last yea.r, the Dominion government had to build two ice breakers, only Canadian firms were asked to tender. What was the outcome? Both contracts were awarded to firms in the Maritime provinces, and I can safely assure beforehand the hon. member for Halifax that these two contracts will hinder instead of fostering the development of ship-building industry in Canada. The Minister of Marine should not be obliged after having asked for tenders, to award the contract to the lowest tenderer. Certain owners of shipbuilding yards are so anxious to find work for their men that they put in tenders even at ruinous prices. It would be better to have the cost of the vessel, on which tenders are sought estimated and refuse to award the contract
should the tender submitted be below the estimates of the department's engineers. The question may be asked why the Canadian shipbuilders cannot compete with those of Europe. This is easily explained. First, the workmen's wages must be taken into consideration. All know that wages paid in Canada to workers in ship-yards are at least double those paid in Europe. We have no blast furnaces or rolling-mills in Canada to produce steel plates which are needed in shipbuilding. These steel plates are imported from England. The freight on these plates must be taken into account. Moreover, the English and European shipbuilding yards have been established for nearly a century and have always been -given the preference on orders from governments or large shipbuilding firms, they therefore have been able to expand more than our Canadian shipbuilding yards.
There are in my riding ship-buiding yards operated by the Davie Shipbuilding Company. The latter were requested, during the war, by the government, to erect a special plant in order to build vessels. This plant has cost more than six million dollars. During war -activities work was plentiful, but since then it has often lacked. It has been rumoured that the Davie Shipbuilding Company, as then organized, made large losses on their shipbuilding contracts during the war. Ever since then, this company has worked mostly for the Canada Steamship Company who are the owners.
During the war the price paid to shipbuilders was $140 per ton, and even at that price Canadian firms could hardly balance their budget. To-day the price has dropped to $60 per ton. How -can we therefore hope that this Canadian industry, whose development has been so costly, can, to-day, compete with that of Europe which has developed gradually and was assisted both by contracts and bonuses from various governments. Simply by giving to this industry the assistance needed and paying a fair price for 'its work. With that end in view the hon. members of this house must impress upon the Minister of Marine the advisability of awarding contracts only to those whose tenders show reasonable profits. It>
is not by fostering competition such as it exists among Canadian builders that we shall find a remedy to our ills.
Take, for instance, a shipbuilding yard whose workers are out of work; you request its owner to tender for the building of a vessel and at the same time you make the same request to the owner of a shipbuilding yard in full activity, immediately you give rise to
Fisheries Act Amendment

competition which will force the former to tender at a price which will allow him to carry on but to carry on miserably. I cannot see any other reason that can explain the ridiculous low prices which the Minister of Marine has received in tenders for the building of the two ice-breakers in question. Can the minister be blamed for accepting those tenders? Evidently not. Had the minister acted otherwise the opposition would not have let slip the opportunity of blaming him for taking the public's money to make a gift of it to a company. For instance, the minister would have been blamed for having made a gift of 1250,000 to the Davie Shipbuilding Company if he had awarded to this company the contract for the building of the first icebreaker, instead of awarding it to the Halifax Shipbuilding Company. It would have been said that the government in acting thus had no other aim but making themselves safe in the Levis riding. Yet our workmen were more in need of work than those of Halifax. And I feel certain that the passing of the estimates of the Marine department would have been delayed for weeks, as it recently happened, for smaller items, when the estimates of the Postmaster General came up. For these reasons, I cannot vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Halifax.
I have but a few comments to add in connection with the contracts awarded to European shipbuilders for the building of two cruisers. The hon. member for Halifax is wrong in blaming the government for not having these two cruisers built in this country. And this is the reason: The Canadian shipbuilders already own machinery which has been very costly to them. Now, to build cruisers, special equipment is necessary, and the ordinary machinery at the disposal of our ship yards is not sufficient for this work. The plates used in the building of cruisers are made of steel in which enters an alloy of chrome and nickel, an alloy so hard1 as to resist boring, cutting, heating and bending with the machinery at present in use in our ship yards. All our shipbuilders would have been forced to order beforehand entirely new machinery which< would have been only used again about ten years hence when the government would have had to replace the cruisers that are being built at present.
To utilize with profit such equipment, it would be necessary for Canada to decide to build a navy. I feel sure that it is not the intention of the hon. member for Halifax to advise the government to take such a

step. I entirely agree with the minister for not having asked our shipbuilders to make a further outlay of SI,000,000 or more 90 as to purchase and erect machinery which would have been utilized exclusively in the building of these two cruisers, the cost of which will not amount to $1,000,000.
If my hon. friend sincerely wishes to help the workmen of our shipbuilding yards, I think it would be better for him to withdraw his amendment and await a more favourable opportunity. I shall then be very pleased to vote with him in favour of any measure which will facilitate the minister in carrying out the promise which he has just made to the house, that is fostering in all possible way the industry of ship-building in Canada.

I have just one brief observation to make. The Minister of National Defence suggested that the government was taking a stand on this question, and that the question was very simple. The royal commission on fisheries decided by a majority of four to one against steam trawling, but the government decides in favour of it. What lead is that to the House of Commons with respect to commissions? Either the commission was composed of men who knew their business better than anyone else or it was a commission which should not have been appointed; it was either a commission of experts or it was not; the experts knew their business or they did not. If they knew their business, then four of them have recommended, in the language of the report, as follows:
We believe that one of the remedies for the present situation is the total prohibition of steam-trawlers from operating from Canadian ports, landing their catch in Canadian ports, or obtaining in Canadian ports coal or supplies. And we recommended that such legislation be enacted as to make such prohibition effective on and after June 1st, 1929.
That commission cost this country $100,000, and that recommendation is made by four of the five commissioners. What lead is it to the House of Commons when the government comes along and says these four men do not know their business but that Mr. Justice Maclean, who is not a fisherman at present, says we must have the trawlers?
That is the real question before this committee. The government tried to divest itself of responsibility by appointing a royal commission. The Minister of Finance said the other day that this country is sick of being governed by commissions, although a few days previously he appointed a commission to deal

Fisheries Act Amendment
with the salaries of technical men in Canada. The Minister of National Defence, confronted with the Duncan report, succeeds in having the government of the day appoint a commission on fisheries composed of five members, of which Mr. Justice Maclean was chairman, with four other members who were said to be gentlemen of wide experience, highly qualified by political and other associations to deal with this problem. Those four gentlemen were Cyrus Macmillan, H.R.L. Bill, Joseph Mom-bourquette and J. G. Robichaud. I am not in a position to place my knowledge against theirs and I ask my hon .friend from Lisgar, who asked a question a moment ago, whether he does not think that those four gentlemen, who were selected by the government which he supports, know more about this matter than we know.
What can I say to my constituents with respect to this matter; what can I say to the public of this country, when four gentlemen named by the government and selected, as I say, because of their wide knowledge, One of them being a college professor, say that steam trawlers should be abolished, while on the other hand a judge of the exchequer court says that action should not be taken? What is this committee to do? The majority is four to one, but now the Minister of National Defence, representing the province of Nova Scotia in the cabinet, says, "I am for Judge Maclean; I agree with him." I leave it to the members of the committee and the country whether or not they think that is giving a lead to public opinion in Canada.
Now I desire to ask the minister one other question. Is it not true that we have renewed the licenses of American fishing boats and that we allow them to enter our Canadian ports to coal, victual, outfit, and land their fish, by an order in council passed within the last three months? I ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if that is not so?
Not on the Atlantic.

Only on the Pacific?
There has been no renewal of the modus vivendi with respect to American fishing boats out of Gloucester?
No.
Then it is clear that they cannot land their catch on the Atlantic?
No.
Nor ice their ships?
No.

Nor obtain supplies of
any kind?
No.

Formerly that was the
case, but now that only applies to the Pacific?
Yes.

The fisheries on the
Atlantic being pretty well cleaned up, now we are to continue this practice until they are wholly cleaned up on the Pacific. In other words, the halibut are to be entirely annihilated, as they have been partially annihilated already, and now that the great fisheries of the Atlantic are becoming exhausted we are to have the same principle applied to the Pacific.
When my hon. friend from Richmond-West Cape Breton and my hon. friend from Inverness are asked as to the position, all they can say, all I can say and all any other Canadian can say is that the government saw fit to select a commission of five members to consider this question, four of whom recommended a certain course of action. The fifth commissioner recommended another action, and the government has taken the opinion of the one commissioner in preference to that of the four. Now what are we to do? The government and the minister will tell us what we must do now. I do submit that this is but an evidence of what you get when you have a condition of this kind in a country like Canada; the sacrifice of principle for the purpose of maintaining power by groups scattered throughout the country. When the groups had been brought together a commission was appointed, and then when the commission made its report, the government did not accept it; the government said that one commissioner was right and the other four were wrong. The hon. minister says that this is but the beginning; it is but the beginning, but it is the beginning of the end of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. leader of the
opposition is very optimistic.

I am not ready to take
too seriously the observations made by the hon. leader of the opposition. I do not think that anyone has ever contended in this house or in the country that every report made by a commission must 'be implemented in its entirety by legislation.	These reports are
merely recommendations which must be studied and looked into by the government
Fisheries Act Amendment

and by the officials of the department. I cannot bring to mind any particular instances, but when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and my friend the leader of the opposition was supporting that government, there were many reports made by commissions, which reports were not adopted in their entirety by the government of the day. I will admit that that is no justification, but it proves that the principle which has been advocated by the hon. leader of the opposition is not possible of application to every case. These commissions are bodies of investigation, that is all, and when my hon. friend says that the minister and the government have chosen between four commissioners and one commissioner, that is not exactly the case. This legislation is the recommendations of a committee of this house. The committee on marine and fisheries dealt with the report of the Atlantic fisheries commission; they dealt with the question of trawlers, and the bill embodies the conclusions arrived at by that committee. The government is merely following the recommendations of the majority of a committee of this house.

The note on page 2 which
indicates the purpose of section 7 reads as follows:
