As I understand it, the recommendation was to the effect that steam trawlers should be abolished.

The word "committee"
refers to the committee on marine and fisheries.
As I understand it, the committee recommended that all ships should be owned either by Canadians or by corporations the majority of whose shareholders were Canadians.
No.

Some committee made that
recommendation.
No.
Then I am quite in error.

The clause in the bill
expresses the conclusions of the committee on marine and fisheries.	.

The Minister of National
Defence (Mr. Ralston) referred to some report having been before the committee-
The minister was referring to the report of the Atlantic fisheries commission.
-that all these ships should be owned by Canadians.

That referred to a bill
which was first introduced in the house but which has been amended by the committee on marine asd fisheries.

Mr. Chairman the remarks
of the Minister of National Defence would tend to give the impression that I was opposed to the beam trawler, when the words of my amendment were not meant to convey that impression. To a certain extent I am in favour of the beam trawler, but the amendment which is now before the committee proposes certain limitations. The hon. leader of the opposition has pointed out that a commission was appointed for the punpose of investigating the condition of the fisheries in the maritime provinces. That commission consisted of three gentlemen who were actively engaged in the fishing industry, a college professor, and a judge of the exchequer court. The three gentlemen who were actively engaged in the fishing industry-
And who were divided in their opinions before they heard the evidence.

along with the college professor, made a certain finding, but the fifth member of the commission, who occupies an independent position, presented a minority report. That royal commission made a report to this government and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that report should have been implemented by this government. But what did they do? Bill No. 26 is brought in, and that bill is discussed by the fisheries committee and a report presented to the house. We have the matter in three successive stages: a royal commission, consisting of supporters or friends of the government; the fisheries committee, which consists of a majority of representatives of the government; and then this committee of the house, which has a majority on the .other side. I am not opposed to the beam trawlers because I believe that they are necessary to the fishing industry, but I am primarily in favour of the shore fisherman. He is entitled to every consideration from this government or any other government; he is entitled to every assistance in the way of protection of the industry by which he earns his livelihood. If the beam trawler is allowed to operate then I say that it should be the product of Canadian shipyards and be built by Canadian workmen.

Fisheries Act Amendment
It may take a little time to bring that result about, but in the interim the question as to whether or not the Shore fishermen can produce sufficient fish to satisfy -the Canadian market can be settled. If they cannot, then there is a justification for the beam trawler, and if the beam trawler is necessary, then it should be the product of Canadian shipyards and of Canadian workmen. The whole responsibility lies upon this government as to whether o-r not they satisfy the fishermen. If they do not make a success of that, it is their responsibility.
It is non-political.

My hon. friend does not
seem to be trying to make it so. He says that it may take a little time to have these vessels Canadian built. I would point out to him that we have to be practical in connection with these matters. If it is going to take a little time, is it not the best course to pursue to give the governor in council power to make regulations, to lay down principles under which licenses may be granted and to consider the very proposal my hon. friend is making, as to whether or not a limitation of time cannot be imposed-my hon. friend does not suggest how long-after which period trawling vessels should be Canadian built? As I said a little while ago, the proposition was made before the fisheries committee that over and above the trawlers now operated, new trawlers should be Canadian built. There cannot be any better method to pursue than to afford an opportunity for the inclusion in the regulations of such a principle if it is considered practical, and if it is not practical, then as my hon. friend says, in the interim- and that- is the word he used-the question whether or not this principle should obtain can be further investigated.
I do not agree with some of the hon. members who have spoken on the other side. They have said that trawlers are absolutely necessary; they lay that down as a basic principle. My opinion is t-hat trawlers are necessary only if they are required to supply the excess demand after the shore fishermen have brought in their supply. That question may have to be and may be considered by the minister in connection with the granting of licenses. If my hon. friend from Halifax is looking at the matter from the practical point of view, this is the best way to bring about the possibility of putting into effect any such suggestion as he has made.

Does the Minister of
Marine and Fisheries not think that to place in the hands of the minister the power of determining the number of licenses he shall issue, is going contrary to the modern ten-
Fisheries Act Amendment

deney? The Chief Justice of England has recently declared in very strong terms against bureaucracy, the bureaucracy that consists in orders in council being passed and government by order in council. Here we have a discretion given to a political minister-and all ministers are political; I am not referring to this minister more than others-a political appointeee, to determine who shall have a license and who shall not. Is that quite right? I think the minister will see where that leads- the pressure of his friends, the opposition of his opponents, and in the end the minister is placed in a position where his efforts will be destroyed. One has only to pick up the daily press to see what happens to men who fearlessly enforce the law; they lost their positions. I put it to the minister whether or not it is a fair thing, in view of what his colleague has said, namely, that this is an experiment, to place the success or failure of that effort in the hands of a minister who necessarily must exercise his power in favour of his political friends and against his political opponents, being in that respect like all other ministers as regards a matter of this kind? The effect of the pressure will be that this experiment, so-called, will be nothing more or less than political effort. Those of us who know the capacity of the Minister of National Defence in dealing with patronage in Nova Scotia know what the inevitable result will be.

I fully realize the difficult
position in which the minister may be placed later on bj- the adoption of this legislation; but somebody has to decide; somebody has to be given the responsibility of deciding a matter of this kind. I think it is for the government to assume the responsibility when they are placed in a position to exercise their judgment. I can assure my hon. friend that the regulations which are provided by that section governing the issuances of licenses to the trawlers, are not going to be drafted without giving the proper consideration and without looking beforehand for advice from all parties concerned in the fishing business. I do not propose to recommend to the governor in council any regulations without having first obtained the advice of and given full opportunity to all those who are interested in the business of fishing to express their views as to the form of these regulations and as regards the power that the minister is given, according to that section, of issuing or refusing licenses. So far as I and the government are concerned, we are not looking towards increasing the number of licenses to trawlers; we are rather looking towards a reduction in the number of those fMr. Bennett.]
licenses. But we thought it would be aa. injustice, unfair, practically to confiscate the trawlers which have so far been operating. Unless very grave circumstances arise or reasons are given, no further licenses are going to be issued for trawlers. I quite realize this is going to be a hard job, but -may I say to my hon. friend with the short experience I have had in that department and in that branch of the service, with the very limited knowledge I may have of that business and the limited knowledge that previous ministers may have had with regard to these technical matters, it is no small affair to administer the fisheries of this country. As my hon. friend has mentioned, representations of all sorts are coming to the minister on every question which is put to him. We have the representations of* the dealers on one side and the fishermen on the other, and we have -to give consideration to the general good of both enterprises and to protect with greater care the interest of the fishermen. This is not a small job and it is not going to be a small job for the minister, but for the short period of time I shall be in that position, I am going to take the chance and I can assure my hon. friend that nobody need be afraid of political interference or of any injustice resulting from the influence of one party or another.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has seen fit to throw out an insinuation which I think was hardly worthy of him.

I intended to make it a
plain statement, not an insinuation at all
There is no Civil Service Act there.

There is no Civil Service Act there, my hon. friend says. That is the excuse that is given; there is no Civil Service Act there. My hon. friend mentioned the other day men who had a contract with the government, and who would be entitled to be paid for life even though they had their contract ended at the age of seventy-five years, but there were men in Nova Scotia who had the same sort of contract with the government and were appointed to hold office during good behaviour, who suddenly found that an act had been passed by the present provincial government changing their tenure to holding office during pleasure, and they were immediately dismissed without cause or investigation. That is the sort of thing we have had in Nova Scotia, and that is the sort of thing I have had to meet in connection with the administration of public affairs there. I want to tell my bon. friend that I would be perfectly happy if he would bring up any case he desires with regard to the administration of patronage or of public business in that province, where he thinks there has been political interference.	.

Mr. Garrison's case will
be here presently.
I shall be very happy now to deal with his case. All I know of it is what I have seen in the newspapers.

Then my hon. friend is
much belied because Mr. Garrison said that there was a telegram sent by the minister.

My hon. friend picks up
anything that happens to be told him and retails it from his prominent place in this house as being the truth. That is an absolute mis-statement. My hon. friend does not know it, but he ought to take a litttle more care to investigate before he makes such statements because he occupies a position of considerable responsibility in this house and in this country, and it is not befitting his office or befitting himself to make these statements without at least some attempt 'at investigation.
So far as this bill is concerned, my hon. friend may be assured that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will have all my best endeavours and cooperation in seeing to it that no political considerations enter into it whatever, but that when licenses are granted, they shall be granted on some fixed principle which applies to everybody and has regard to the best interests of the industry and of the men and women who are engaged in it.

I say that there is
nothing too small for the minister to interfere with in Nova Scotia. I say that deliberately, and if you want evidence of it we had it this session when at the public accounts committee he as a minister of the crown sat in that committee and watched its proceedings to protect MacMillan. We have further evidence-this is not the time and place, but the evidence will be brought forward before this house prorogues-in connection with the case of MacMillan, who is the political henchman of the Minister of National Defence, and is well known so to be. The minister's assumption of virtue in matters political is belied by the record, and I say that the people of Nova Scotia know it and they understand it and that is the reason he usually sits for one constituency for one term only and no more.
With respect to this particular matter, a large measure of power, life or death with respect to property is vested in the minister. The minister says what is perfectly true, that political pressure is exercised with respect to these matters. We have had evidence of it in this house within the last two weeks. In the one case when a minister was asked by one of his employees for an investigation, he referred it to his colleague whose signature had dispossessed that man of his position. Naturally, every government must play the game in that way. A minister must support his colleague, and when his colleague takes responsibility, he in turn must support his colleague's view, and that was what was done when the situation arose as it did the other day, and the man failed to obtain an investigation because the minister affected said no.
When the Lord Ohief Justice of England was directing attention the other day to these bureaucracies, he pointed out that legislation in parliament in recent years has taken the form of skeleton acts, leaving to the governor or king in council or to a department great powers, and that that was disastrous to democracy and the effect of it was ruinous. Political pressure is invoked, and the result is that a man to save his property must agree to support the administration of the day. That is What happens, and you see men who are Conservative to-day suddenly voting Liberal to-morrow and vice versa, because the government of the day makes it impossible for them to continue to support a party that is opposed to the government if they want to get what they desire and require. It is not a case at all of this one particular instance, for this is but one of many, and
Fisheries Act Amendment

when I point out the fact it is merely something that every man may see for himself if he studies conditions in this country, Regulations are passed, and these regulations permit the very thing that in my judgment must be stopped if we are going to preserve the democratic principles of t'he institutions that we are living under. To say that a man must support a government or he will not get what he wants is but a manifestation of a principle which is very, very destructive to our institutions.
Then there is patronage. The Minister of National Defence says that patronage in Nova Scotia arises because of the fact that there is a government in power in that province that does not support this government; that the provincial government exercises patronage against this government's supporters, and he is therefore pressed to do it as against Conservatives in the federal field. I pointed out that there is no Civil Service Act in that province. The minister says there is a provision in the Civil Service Act that if a man engages in political activities he loses his position. That provision is in the act, but the minister does not for a moment think that there is any difference in political parties with respect to this question of patronage. The pressure is the same whether it is a Conservative or a Liberal government. But what we are endeavouring to do is to remove the possibility of that pressure being exercised, and I say that it is improper for such a wide power to be left to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The Minister of National Defence, from Nova Scotia, says that he will do what he can, but when his friends insist on a certain thing being done, you will have exactly the situation that we have had many evidences of. Remember, we are not dealing with generalities. We bad a great commission that sat here, and we saw the very great .pressure that was exercised-members of parliament, ministers, pressure of that kind-and it will continue so long as you afford the means. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks me to explain the bill. I would have thought this would be ratiher unnecessary, because it is absolutely similar to the bill which has passed this house three or four times only ta meet an unfortunate fate in another place. This house is committed to the bill after having adopted it, as I have said, three or four times.
There is perhaps much misapprehension as to the effect of the bill. It is far from having the effect of wiping out the crime of sedition from the criminal code. Its purpose is to replace the law as it was prior to the session of 1919. The crime of sedition existed then and wiil still be in the criminal code after this bill has become law. Under the present section 132 of the criminal code the crime of sedition is divided into seditious wiords, which are words expressive of a seditious intention; seditious libel, which is a libel expressive of a seditious intention; and, thirdly, seditious conspiracy, which is an agreement between two or more persons to carry into execution a seditious intention. As the house will observe, the seditious intention plays an important part in the crime of sedition, whether this crime consist in words, writing or conspiracy. The crime of sedition under the British law is a crime under the common law, and it has never been found advisable to define exactly what circumstances and what facts constitute sedition; this has been left to the courts, judges and juries. There was a disposition in the English draft bill to fix a definition, but it was found better not to do so; and here in Canada our criminal code,

as originally drawn and introduced into parliament, contained a clause defining a seditious intention. Blit after much debate in the Canadian parliament it was deemed advisable not to try to have a restrictive definition but to leave the offence of sedition as it was under the common law. And of course the meaning is very general. As has been stated, sedition embraces everything, whether by word, deed or writing, which is calculated to disturb the tranquility of the state. It was so general in its meaning, as first introduced, that parliament found it advisable to place in the code a section safeguarding freedom of speech. That section, which appeared in the criminal code until 1919, and which we are asking now to reinstate, is rather the most important part of this bill. Section 133 of the criminal code as it was in force before 1919, and which section 2 of this bill is intended to reinstate, reads:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious . intention only because he intends in good faith,-
"(a) to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or,
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom, or of any part of it, or of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada, or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in the state; or,
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects."
I freely confess that I am at a loss to understand why this section was repealed in 1919. Surely nothing therein described could be an offence; the citizens of a country have the right to criticize measures of the government, and to try to show to the people of that country that the sovereign has been misled by his officers, or something to that effect. This safeguard we wish to reinstate in our criminal code.
The second purpose is to repeal the sections which are now consolidated in section 98 of the present criminal code and which were enacted at the same session in 1919, purporting to define certain acts, words or publications as being seditious. As I stated before, these are absolutely unnecessary because the offence of sedition as it exists under the common law, and as it is already in the criminal code, embraces all the things which might have been mentioned in that section. It did not improve the law; far from it. On the other hand, it has been strongly resented and found objectionable by a large section of the citizens

Criminal Code Amendment
of Canada. As a matter of fact, since I have been a member of the government it has been my privilege to attend every delegation which has met the government each year from the Trades and Labour Council, from the railroad brotherhoods and from other labour organizations, who have all represented to the government their strong resentment of this change in the criminal code. Indeed, they have called attention to the fact that the word "force" as used in that section has been interpreted by certain gentlemen as being applicable to a sympathetic strike. It has been argued that a sympathetic strike constitutes a kind of force, and organized labour, rightly or wrongly, believe that that section as it stands may be used as a means of putting obstacles in their way and denying them the right to strike when they deem it wise to do so. It has been represented to us that organized labour at times cannot find halls for their meetings because the owners are afraid that by renting the hall to such labour associations they may come under the provisions of this section. I may remark that it is rather extraordinary to give to the commissioner of mounted police, who after all is a police officer, the right without warrant to authorize his men to go and take hold of property, either real or personal, on mere suspicion. This, it seems to me, is an extraordinary provision which one cannot find in the code of any other country. I repeat that the law as it was, and as we want to reinstate it, is sufficiently strong to punish the crime of sedition in whatever manner it may be committed.
There is another misapprehension I would like to correct; far from this being done at the instance of or to please the communists, I may say that if I thought this amendment would have the effect of helping them I certainly would not be fathering this bill, but this change is requested not by the disorderly elements in the country but by organized labour, by the men who have been helpful in maintaining peace and order in our industrial relations, and that is why I am introducing the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I have only one observation
to make. The legislation in question has been on the statute books of this country for ten years, and during that time no prosecution has been entered under it. Therefore it has adversely affected no interest, nor' has it done harm to any person. We are now asked to repeal it because, in my judgment, there has been a great misapprehension on the part of organized labour as to what it really meant.
In essence it is merely an effort to preserve the life of the state by making more definite and clear the conditions under which men may carry on propaganda of whatever kind they may desire to spread. There is no limitation or restriction placed upon legitimate propaganda; there is no restriction upon those who desire to criticize our institutions or to support by peaceful means any change in the conditions under which they live, but the section was drawn for the purpose of meeting a condition which was very real, not only in this country but in others, a condition which we hope has disappeared but which may recur. The essential subsection is as follows:
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada, by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed pnrpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
Then follow subsections dealing with other phases of the same matter. It will be observed, therefore, that there is no limitation placed upon peaceful associations, upon propaganda, or upon any effort within reasonable limits to bring about needed changes in the body politic, but it does aim to prevent these unlawful associations from disseminating the doctrine of force in connection with our changes in our constitution or institutions, and I say it i3 helpful to have upon the statute books of this country laws which will protect us from that form of propaganda.
As ten years have passed without any charges being brought under this section it may be taken that the deterrent effect has prevented such propaganda. I recall reading in the newspapers during the last few years reports of gentlemen making speeches and saying, "Of course, we do not advocate that these changes should be brought about by physical force." I have no doubt that the reason for those statements was this section of the criminal code, and to that extent it has been useful; it has prevented the extremist from carrying on the operations which he might have carried on, and no injustice has been worked to any person. So it cannot be said that it has curbed reasonable criticism, lessened freedom of speech or in any sense deprived peaceful citizens of any rights which they should enjoy with regard to the carrying on of any reasonable propaganda having for

Criminal Code Amendment

its purpose the persuasion of other people to think as they think. For that reason I say this is not the time when there should be a change of this kind, especially in view of conditions which have been brought to our attention since this house met, conditions which we know and which the minister knows from reports made to him from time to time are not wholly absent from this Dominion but which we hope will become less as the days go by and men realize that no good1 purpose is to be served by an effort to subvert the laws of the state or reach their ends by other than peaceful means.
If I thought any good purpose could be served by repealing this section of the act I would support this action, but since no harm has been done by this section, no good will be done by its repeal. No useful end will be served by making it possible for those so disposed to carry on their propaganda in a more reckless manner, with less hesitation in the expression of their ideas as to the means necessary to attain their ends.
That is the only observation I have to make with respect to this legislation. If there were any limitation as to the power of expression by the humblest citizen of this Dominion as to the desirability of effecting changes in any industrial activity or in the government of the day, certainly I would not support any such limitation, but as this section aims to prevent the application of force to attain that end, it serves a useful purpose as a deterrent, and it should not be repealed.
Motion agreed to on division, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Unlawful associations.

With regard to this bill I
might say that I .personally made an intensive study of the common law as it stood in 1918. I was then associated with the Department of Justice, and we found it impossible to secure convictions under the law as it then stood against those who were actively advocating the use of force to overturn the existing governmental institutions of this country. If this section is repealed I say with considerable confidence that those who desire to advocate force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic changes, within Canada, will have a great deal more freedom to do so. Those who advocate force, violence or physical injury for the purpose of bringing about governmental or constitutional reforms in this country should be amenable to the criminal [Mr. Bennett.3
law of Canada, because they are really the people who become responsible for rhe use of force for such purposes, by advocating it and inciting others to commit acts of violence for that purpose. Personally I am against the complete repeal of the present section 98, although possibly it might well be modified in some particulars.
While I am on my feet I might refer to section 133a. I do not see any objection to adding this section to the present criminal law of the country. I think we are all agreed that the matters dealt with in these several clauses should not foe deemed to indicate a seditious intent, but personally I think that a complete repeal of section 98 is not in the best interests of this Dominion. I have no animosity or feeling of hostility to the labour movement in any way, shape or form, but if we are to preserve in times of crisis the institutions of this country, it must be made a crime to advocate the overthrow of those institutions by force in a democratic country such as this where complete liberty of moral suasion is permitted and upheld.
Has there been, at any time during Canada's history, an attempt on the part of any organization to overthrow any constituted form of government?

For a short time I was
associated with the Department of Justice with the nominal title of director of public safety, and I came in touch with scores of such cases. If the records of the department have been preserved it will be seen that there were many such cases.
Mr. WARD. What kind of governmsnt were they trying to overthrow?
They were trying to overthrow the form of government which we have in Canada to-day, no doubt about it.
Civic, provincial or federal?

Civic, provincial and federal. There came to my attention evidence of foreign funds which had been supplied to a very considerable extent during the last years of the war; foreign agents and aliens, who were resident outside of this country, governmental and otherwise, were sending funds into this country to establish printing presses from one end of the country to .the other, for the issuance of propaganda inciting to force, and in saying that I speak from personal knowledge. There were very few prosecutions during that time, but I communicated with some of the leaders of those movements and asked

Fish Traps-Mr. Neill
them to come to Ottawa, and I told them in a most emphatic manner that unless they desisted from those methods they would have to be met with more severe enactments than were then upon the statute books of the country. Those who were propagating that incitation to violence were men who had come to this country from foreign countries provided with foreign funds to be used for such purposes.

Has the hon. member ever
seen any evidence of success on the part of those so-called foreign organizations?

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Seditious words, punishment.

In many cases it is
within the discretion of a judge to impose a very severe penalty and it has been found that that option serves a very useful purpose, and I cannot understand why a reduction has been made from twenty years to two years.

speechtext:
It is for the purpose of
making the law as it was in 1919; two years was the penalty at that time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss a matter of some importance to British Columbia as a whole and of very great importance particularly to a number of people in that province. It is a matter that I intended to bring up on the estimates of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), and I have sat here patiently, 78594-2221
or with such measure of patience as one can command at this season of the year, for three whole days from eleven o'clock in the morning to eleven o'clock at night, for the appropriate item to be brought up. But there has been so much delay and so many interruptions that I may not be here when it comes up. Of course the matter can be discussed in committee when and if we do reach that stage eventually. I understand, speaking at this particular juncture, that I am entitled to speak for more than forty minutes and this would be my opportunity to get back at the advocates of the forty-minute rule and speak for a couple of days. But I want the support of the house generally and of the government and I understand this course would not meet with the approval of hon. members. Therefore, if I can get the attention of the house for thirty or forty minutes, I think I can confine my remarks to that time.
The matter to which I wish to refer concerns fish trap licenses for salmon in British Columbia. Some months ago the government appointed a commission to ascertain whether it would be in the public interest to allow the use of salmon traps in the northern part of British Columbia adjacent to the boundary line between British Columbia and Alaska. The commissioner has reported and I have his report under my hand. To put the matter briefly, he recommends the use of fish traps. I want to give a number of reasons why the report of that commissioner should not be accepted.
The essential objection is that the use of fish traps will eliminate the working fishermen of British Columbia. Last year 14,000 fishing licenses were issued in that province. It is well known that a man does not live to himself alone; it has been calculated that a working miner, between his own dependents and those who make their living out of his wages, supports seven or eight persons. If, therefore, those 14,000 license holders were put out of business, something like 100,000 people would be involved. I do not suggest that that would be the immediate result if the trap licenses were granted in this particular area to-day or this year; because probably there would be only fifteen or twenty traps and it might not affect more than a couple of thousand or twenty-five hundred men. But as surely as day follows dark, if the principle is once granted there it must inevitably be accepted elsewhere in British Columbia and this will lead to the ultimate elimination of those fishermen and of those dependert upon them.

speechtext:
Possibly "automatic" is the
word .that I should 'have used instead of pump gum, but the principle is the same. If you go out shooting and use an automatic instead of an ordinary gun you can imagine the slaughter, anyone who was seeking to kill, regardless of consequences so far ns game preservation is concerned, would readily say that it was the
best weapon he could have because it is the most destructive. We know what would inevitably happen in a very short time if it were used by many people.
It may be said, and it has been said, that . they have traps in Alaska. So they have, in large numbers; and what has been the result? The almost total annihilation of the salmon industry. The conditions were such that a commissioner, Mr. O'Malley, a very capable administrator, was appointed with wide powers to do exactly what he liked. He was an autocrat. All he was required to do was to restore the fisheries of Alaska to some semblance of their old state. The first thing that he did was to turn his attention to traps. The cannery men saw it coming, and they got together and presented a nice little plan to him by which they would voluntarily cut down their traps. There was some dispute among them as to just which traps should be cut down, and the commissioner said, "I can settle this quite easily. I will cut them all out," and in that particular year he cut them practically all out in one particular district.
I have not the details, but in southeastern Alaska, the worst district in regard to being over-fished, he cut out I think over 100 traps, and he is going to do away with more next year. According to the Pacific Fisherman, an American publication, he is going to extend that principle to four other areas, which are the remaining areas in which trap fishing is permitted. He intends to cut out ninety-five in that area and reduce the size of the traps, and in another area he is going to cut out seventeen. He is going in very heavily for the reduction of traps, in some areas cutting them out almost entirely and in others reducing them extensively, because of the destructive, almost annihilative effects of trap fishing.
In British Columbia we do not need any more destructive weapons to take our fish; we have too many already. The catch is getting bigger every year, not by the increase of fish, but by more intensive fishing, and we certainly do not want to increase our weapons for fishing; on the contrary we find it necessary to restrict them.
The purse seine is very little better in its destructive operations than the trap, but still it is not quite so bad, and we have formed a large number of areas-last year eighteen were added-in which no person may use a purse seine, the waters being reserved entirely for gill net fishing and trolling, which give the fish a much better chance to get away. In addition to that, we have a regularly weekly close season of forty-eight hours. We
Fish Traps-Mr. Neill

have a further system of restriction which is known as the progressive weekly close season. The chief inspector sizes up a certain area and says from his experience, "I think the number of gill nets that that area could properly stand with a proper escapement of fish would be, say, fifty gill nets, or so many seines." He says, "If fifty gill nets are put in that area the weekly close season will be forty-eight hours, but if fifty-five are put in the weekly close season will be sixty hours." He goes on in that progression, so that if one hundred gill nets are put in, the weekly close sea>son would be seventy-two hours or more, and he is prepared to carry on that progression until, a certain number of gill nets being used there would be only one day's fishing a week, which would be entirely unprofitable to those doing it. That is what we are doing now without any fish traps. We .certainly do not need to add to our already overstocked weapons of fishing what is admittedly the most destructive method known to the human mind for catching fish.
To give you an idea of what people there think about this matter, let me read a wire that I have received from the chairman of a meeting that was held at Prince Rupert:
Be it resolved that we the citizens of Prince Rupert assembled in public meeting and representing all occupations and walks of life are strongly opposing permission being granted to operate any salmon fish traps anywhere in the northern British Columbia salmon fishing district No. 2 on the ground that salmon traps, if permitted to operate will endanger livelihood of large portion of British Columbia's population. Letter follows.
In addition to that, I have a petition here that I am presenting to the minister privately because, not being correctly worded, it cannot be presented formally to the bouse. It reads as follows:
To the Minister of Fisheries of the government of
The Hon. Mackenzie King,
Ottawa, Canada.
We, the undersigned citizens of British Columbia, do hereby petition your department to prohibit all fish traps in British Columbia and also prohibit all seining of salmon between Chatham Point light and Victoria, British Columbia, taking in all waters in the gulf of Georgia and inlets leading into same.
The object being to put a stop to the wholesale destruction of young salmon by these methods of fishing. All of the adult salmon can be taken by gill nets and spoons without the slaughtering of the immature.
The above mentioned area is a natural feeding ground for all species of young salmon for the first period of their lives.
Hon. members will notice that it goes even further than asking for the abolition of traps alone. That is signed by something like

eleven hundred people. The man who sends it to me says he is forwarding :by a future mail two or three more petitions much more fully signed.
Now we come to the report-such as it is. I want to say that if the government paid more than a dollar and six bits for the report then tile people of Canada are stung to the extent it exceeds that sum; it is not worth any more than that. It consists of twenty pages. I have not time to deal with it all; I do not need to. I will deal with the recommendations. I will quote two or three of them and show how those recommendations not only contradict each other, but contradict other portions of the report. A great deal of the report consists of commonplaces, which to people familiar with the fishing industry and the conditions there might almost be termed platitudes. It does show that at least the commissioner has failed to grasp the real genesis of the situation out there. He makes five recommendations. There is really only one; the rest of them are reasons for that recommendation or padding. This is the first one:
That traps for the catching of salmon to a limited number be permitted or allowed in the following described area:-
Then he gives the area by its geographical description, which I need not repeat. It will be noticed he says, "that traps for the catching of salmon to a limited number be permitted -V That, is, not the traps are to be limited; oh no; but "traps for the catching of salmon to a limited number".

Let me deal with that. I say most emphatically it will and it must curtail fishing by other gear. There are two ways by which curtailment will be brought about. First, nearly all these seines are either owned directly by the cannery, which operates a

Fish Traps-Mr. Neill
paid crew, or financed by the cannery, which equips the fishermen on a percentage basis. No cannery is going to put oeines into the water or finance fishermen if it can get traps, because traps are cheaper and more convenient for the cannery; just as it is obvious that a man out to make a killing among ducks or deer regardless of consequences would not use an ordinary gun if he were allowed an automatic. I would refer to the evidence in which a man came forward and said he had gone to some cannery and asked for a boat and net. That is the usual practice, the cannery supplying the boat and net on a percentage basis. But the manager refused the man's request, stating they did not care about gill netters now as they had traps. He gave this as an instance of the viewpoint of the companies-and a very natural one indeed. Why should they bother about outfitting men with gill nets and purse seines when they can have a number of traps? That shows it would curtail the employment of these other fishermen, because they would not themselves be able to buy gill nets or purse seines, and no company would be anxious to give them the necessary financial backing. The second reason why it would curtail the other gear is this. We are now restricting the areas. We are searching about to restrict the number of fish now being taken. We are cutting down the fishing sometimes to four days a week. Two years ago it was necessary in the middle of the fishing season to put on a close season of two weeks. The canneries and the fishermen were in the midst of their operations, they had to cease work and leave all their equipment idle. This involved a disastrous expense. It was found necessary two years ago-and I believe it was justified-to put on that close season. So you see, as I have said before, we are restricting them all we can, and now on top of that over-fished water- too much gear in the water-it is proposed to throw in unlimited traps. This is the most destructive method known. It will discourage the use of gill nets and purse seines, and the inevitable result must be more close seasons, because there will be too many fish taken and the fish inspector will come along and say, "We must put on an extra twenty-four or forty-eight hour a week close season." This would involve hardships, especially to the working fishermen, because an idle trap affects only four men, but if the fisherman has to be idle three or four days a week he cannot make a living fishing the other one or two days. It came out in the evidence that on
an average the traps employ four men. I calculate that one trap would replace twenty or twenty-five fishermen. But that does not mean there would be only twenty-five fishermen out of a job because, as I said before, he has his wife and family dependent on him, and he has other men incidentally depending on his wages. It is calculated that seven people are dependent on one fisherman; that would be something like 150 people would be out of employment for every trap that was operated; for you must remember, Mr. Speaker, that a trap does not have its hair cut, it does not buy clothes, it does not go to the movies; it simply stays there and does not cost anything when idle. But these other fishermen give other people work, all the inhabitants of the little towns depend for their living on the money earned by those fishermen.
To show that this is not only my opinion but the opinion of the commissioner, may I turn to page 17. This is not something I am twisting out of the document; these are his exact words:
The fishermen were able to convince me that traps would reduce the number of fish they would catch, and an elimination to some extent of the number of men engaged in the fishing business. This Mr. Hagar concedeslie is the manager of the company.
-the number so eliminated would naturally depend on the number of traps put in the water.
Naturally so. And he is going to allow unlimited traps; so the number of men thrown out of employment would be unlimited. After reading that statement, surely it is a joke for him to say that it will not appreciably curtail the number of gear now in the water.
Now we come again to his defence-I desire to be polite. He says:
Canadian traps. . . will result in catching a share of the salmon now being caught by American traps and which otherwise would be lost to Canada.
I call particular attention to those words, "otherwise lost to Canada." That, Mr. Speaker, is begging the whole question, because I may explain the cannery men's argument is that these would-be traps are placed on the border line between British Columbia and Alaska. In that particular place Alaska, we might say for the purpose of comparison, lies north of British Columbia. The cannery men contend that the fish go from the south to the north, and if we do not put in these
Fish Traps-Mr. Neill

traps, then the fish will go on into American waters and be caught with American traps. This, so to speak, is the "last chance" at them.
Now, the commissioner appears to have swallowed that argument, stock, lock and barrel. His acceptance is based entirely on a bald assertion by a cannery man that that is so. But the fishermen come along and say the opposite. They say that the fish are going south and that therefore Canadian traps would take fish which would otherwise go, not into American traps, but into the Skeena and other rivers in British Columbia to be caught by gill nets and trollers. Those are the two points of difference. The cannery men say that the fish go north while the fishermen contend that they go south, and the commissioner throws his whole weight into the argument of the cannery men.

But surely the facts are
known as to which way they go.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
They are to some extent,
and I will explain that in a moment. But as between the two, what little is known is emphatically on the side of the argument that the fish go south. Here is a report on Pacific salmon migration by Professor H. Charles Williams, DSc., F.R.S.E., a technical and highly educated man, who is not going to throw his weight one way or the other but undertakes to record the facts as he sees them. He tagged 659 fish, and I may explain to those who are not familiar with it just what this means. They take the salmon when newly caught and put a clip into its tail or one of its fins and then turn it loose, and when it is ultimately caught valuable information is obtained as to where it has been in the meantime and where it is going. This is a new method only recently adopted. Now according to this report only 135 of the 659 were recaptured that season, and of that number 80 per cent were caught in British Columbia waters and 20 per cent in American waters. He actually gives us a map showing the course run by every fish from the time it was first tagged until it was finally caught. One was caught 100 miles south inside of twenty-four hours; in other words, it was travelling at an average of 100 miles a day. As I say, 80 per cent were taken the second time in British Columbia waters. This man's report ought to be good because it is a definite, unbiased and scientific statement, and he asserts that 80 per cent were taken in the waters of British Columbia, proving, so far as our knowledge goes, that the fish were going south. Therefore this theory of putting in

last chance traps is entirely unsound, and the argument that the fish would "otherwise be lost" is not based on the facts.
The third reason the commissioner gives is this:
The Department of Fisheries with traps in this area will be in a better position to carry on a more intensive system of tagging, and for the next few years study the run of fish from Wales island and Dogfish, that is, whether and to what extent they are making for Canadian and United States waters.
You will note that he says it will enable them to go in for more intensive tagging. He is proposing to put in traps-perhaps twenty -at a cost of $150,000 in order to catch a few fish to be tagged-a few hundred or a thousand fish which could be caught just as well with seine or troll. Now, Mr. Speaker, when we want roast chicken we do not burn down the hen house and its contents. Is there any need of investing $150,000 to establish a destructive method of fishing in order to catch a few fish to be tagged when experience shows that they can be captured just as well by seine or trollers? It is done off the west coast of Vancouver island; I have seen them do it with the troll and they have been quite successful. They did not need to use any traps. Further, it is stated, we shall be enabled to decide to what extent the fish are making for Canadian or for American waters. In that sentence is to be found proof of what I have said, namely, that the commissioner, with al'l due respect to him, has failed to grasp the situation as it exists. He is going to allow traps to be used for an unlimited period and in unlimited numbers for the purpose of taking fish by a very destructive method in order that some of them may be tagged to determine whether traps should be allowed or not. Do you grasp that? Traps, with their iniquitous capture of these fish, are to be allowed in order to determine by means of tagging the fish whether the traps should be allowed or not. The last time I heard reasoning of that sort was at a country fair and by a quack doctor selling patent medicines. Would it not be better to continue the existing system of tagging with a view to demonstrating whether the traps should be allowed or not?
Now we come to the other recommendations. No. 2 is, that applications for licenses should be open to all. Well, applications for licenses have been open to all for the last twelve years. That policy was adopted by the Conservatives in 1918 and has been continued ever since; it is known as the open door policy. So that when he recommends that applications be open to all he is merely re-

Fish Traps-Mr. Neill
peating a commonplace. Mind you, it is not a question of putting in two or three traps; the New England Fish Company would be content with three. But every other cannery man in that vicinity would also demand fish traps; and as a matter of fact they say plainly that if one gets them they will all get them.
The third recommendation is that licenses be granted only for a specified time until the results of the tagging operations have become known. Note that: a specified time. But what is a specified time? He does not say. It may be a year or a decade or fifty years. However, he recommends that the licenses be granted only for a specified time until the results of the tagging operations are known. He gives the show away in that sentence, because he admits he does not know whether the traps should be there or not. But he says, in effect: "In the meantime, let them operate with this destructive method until we find out by the tagging operations whether the traps should be allowed or not." Is that not putting the cart before the home? Why not let the fish traps wait until the present system proves conclusively whether or not the suggestion is correct that the fish are going south?
The fourth recommendation is that no license granted in any sense creates a vested interest in the owner for any period longer than is mentioned in the license. If that is not a platitude I have never heard one. If I rent a house for ten years I know that the house does not belong to me at the end of that period; but there is no need for anybody to tell me that.
The fifth and last recommendation is that the opening of areas specified in recommendation No. 1 is in no sense to be regarded as a precedent to be cited or acted upon in respect to any other areas or territories in this or any other fishing district in British Columbia. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would point this out: You cannot establish a precedent and then by a wave of the hand say it is not a precedent. If I commit murder and formally announce that the deed is not to be regarded as murder, I cannot get. away with it; the corpse is there, justice is demanded, and the law will step in and brush aside my sophistry. A precedent once established is there for all to point at, and it will be pointed to. A week or two ago I used an illustration which perhaps I might now repeat. Was it not said by the Conservative party, and properly, that their legislation in 1918, in regard to the good roads grant was not to be considered a precedent? Yet every member who spoke on the subject a few months ago sooner or later cited that very precedent. I will tell you why the
commissioner makes this statement. He wants to conciliate public sentiment and allay alarm, because the people are afraid that this principle, once established in the north, will spread to the south. And it is for that very reason that I take so keen an interest in the matter. This particular district is away beyond my own, buc our people are terribly afraid of thi3 thing called a precedent; because once it is established that it is right to have traps up there, the next thing will be to have them in the southern waters in the district I represent.
Now it may be said that I am unjustifiably suspicious, that I am an alarmist, that I am pleading a special cause and for that reason making the strongest case I can. Not at all.
I have evidence here to show that it will be only a matter of a very short time, if traps are granted in the north, before the precedent will be cited in the south. And here is the evidence to show that before that policy is actually adopted traps in the south are being recommended. I quote from a newspaper report of the evidence:
Mr. Hagar not only advocated the establishment of fish traps in northern waters, but also throughout the province.
There is the handwriting on the wall. Before ever traps are granted in the north, he says, "You have given them in the north and we must have them in the south as well." Am I not justified in asking, if they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?
Now, sir, it is up to the government. Some hon. gentlemen may ask why the government should not accept the report of the commission. Possibly that should be done in most cases, but not in the case of a wabbly, stillborn report like this, which contradicts itself in its own recommendations and in other ways. This afternoon one of the members from the maritime provinces was criticizing the government, and when a member of the government challenged him to define his policy in regard to the question under discussion the hon. member replied that he would not do so, that the responsibility must rest with the government. That was a politician's answer, of course, because it left him free to find fault with whatever action the government took. I am not afraid to take the responsibility or the blame for anything I advocate; I have the courage of my convictions. Of course it would pay me better in a political way to let the government go ahead, and do wrong, because then I could yell " crook and scandal " during the election campaign, but where would my district be
Fish Traps-Mr. Neill

left? I would rather see the government do the right thing now even if they get credit for it instead of myself.
Here is the question: As I have said, there are 14,000 working fishermen licensed this year; with their families and those indirectly depending upon them, including the farmers- because they do not eat fish exclusively; they must have eggs and butter and milk-and the town people who are also dependent upon the earnings of these fishermen, we might take it that 100,000 people would be affected. We want these people, Mr. Speaker; we have them now and we want to keep them because they are a sturdy, desirable class of citizens. Are we going to wipe them out and leave our shores barren except for a few fish traps placed at strategic points in order to swell the coffers of an alien corporation? I think I can safely say that I represent the views of every fisherman in British Columbia; they are a unit in their opposition to these fish traps. Practically all the people of northern British Columbia in the neighbourhood of Prince Rupert, irrespective of politics or occupation, are of the same opinion in this matter, and judging from the petition I have presented and from others which I could produce, there are a great many people in the southern part of British Columbia also opposed to these fish traps.
Now I have practically finished; the decision is up to the government. I beg and implore them-yes, I even warn them-to put people before pocket, men before money, in this case and let the decision be made on that principle.
I do not want to be melodramatic; I do not want to use sensaitional language, but I am trying to find words which will impress upon the government the seriousness of this situation. I am sorry if I am unable to emphasize sufficiently the importance of the matter, but I believe, and more than that I hope, that a curse will rest upon this government, certainly politically, if they take away the livelihood of these people in order to produce a few quicker and fatter dividends for an alien corporation, because that is practically what it amounts to, no matter how it may be wrapped up and regardless of how it may be explained or camouflaged. I might almost paraphrase the American orator-William Jennings Bryan, and say: We must not, we shall not and we dare not crucify our British Columbia fishermen on a cross of increased dividends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am sorry that this question has come up so prematurely, because it is a complex matter 
fraught with very great interest to thousands of fishermen on the Pacific coast. The commission which sat in Prince Rupert and Vancouver some weeks ago to consider the question of the advisability of allowing traps to be installed along the international waters in the northern part of district No. 2, was composed of one gentleman, Judge Ellis. I found it very difficult to get information with regard to the origin of this commission, as to who appointed it, who authorized it and so on. As far as I can gather, Mr. Speaker, it was done by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), who was anxious to settle once and for all the question of the advisability of permitting traps in these waters.
I have before me a letter which was handed to me by the hon. member for New Westminster, (Mr. McQuarrie), who is not here, with the request that I read it in the house. This letter refers to fish traps, and is as follows:
New Westminster, B.C., May 18/29. Mr. W. G. McQuarrie, M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed to call your attention to the recent action of the Department of Marine and Fisheries with respect to salmon traps and to ask you to support the fishermen in their opposition to the same. Following are the facts as the fighermen know them:
Late in 1927, in October or November, a delegation of salmon eanners and fishermen held two meetings with Hon. P. J. A. Cardin and asked that a royal commission be appointed to investigate the salmon fishing industry in British Columbia with a view to recommending remedial action of some sort. This was opposed by W. A. Found, and the commission was not granted. After departure from Ottawa of fishermen delegates eanners put forward set of requests of their own, unknown to the fishermen. The man who arranged the two meetings of the joint committee with Mr. Cardin was an attorney of Vancouver named J. E. Ellis, evidently retained by the eanners, as the fishermen did not retain him.
Recently, without fishermen having the remotest idea that such a thing had been applied for, announcement was made in Vancouver that Judge Ellis was named as a royal commission to investigate and determine whether it would be in the "public interest" to allow the establishment of salmon traps in Canadian waters adjacent to the Alaskan boundary. In the "public interest" and "adjacent" were two terms that stuck in the craws of the Prince Rupert men. where the first meetings were held. Naturally, fishermen opposed traps and eanners favoured them. At the Vancouver meeting Mr. Ellis, when questioned who asked for the appointment of himself as a commission, said he did not know, he merely received word by wire from Ottawa to make the investigation and report thereon. However, A. L. Hager, president Canadian Fishing Company, was not so reticent . or ignorant, and stated his company probably was responsible for the appointment of a com-

Fish Traps-Mr. Brady
mission to see if his firm would not be allowed to operate traps at Wales island which they purchased some years ago from M. Desbrisay and were stopped from operating them. Therefore it appears to the fishermen that the Department of Marine and Fisheries has, under guise of a general investigation, appointed a commission for the specific purpose of giving the Canadian Fishing Company right to operate certain traps, and so that will not appear too raw to the proletariat, etc., a few more trap sites will be given to other concerns, and then the general scramble will be on again.
Wm. E. Maiden.
Secretary, B.C.F.P.A.
Then he asks that the hon. member for New Westminster support the fishermen in their contention that traps should not be installed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, hon. members were privileged to read the report of Judge Ellis together with the evidence given by the various witnesses; if hon. members could understand the attitude of the representatives of the two apposing sides, the one against and the other advocating traps, together with the summing up by Judge Ellis and his recommendation in favour of the installation of fish traps along the international boundary, I have no hesitation in saying after reading the report that no one unprejudiced could possibly claim that all the convincing evidence produced at the meetings of that commission held in Prince Rupert was given by the representatives of the fish traps.
I have taken from the report a few of the reasons which were advanced as to why the traps should be installed. I am very sorry that I had not more time at my disposal to go through this report thoroughly, because we are not dealing with a local issue. I wish to impress that upon the house; the question of fish traps in Canadian waters is not a local issue, it is outside the realm of any local condition; it is international in its scope and demands a broad international mind to deal with it in order that justice may be done to both sides arguing this question. Here are some of the reasons given by the advocates of fish traps in support of their claim that traps should be installed in these northern waters.
The first reason given was that the traps represent the modern trend in fishing. In American waters to-day the trap is the one and only, up-to-date, scientific machine for catching salmon with very little difficulty. It is quite true that it is the modern trend in fishing.
The second argument offered was that a better grade of fish was caught. That is true likewise. The fish get into the traps of their own accord, and they are in perfect condition when caught.	.
The third argument was that traps would enable us better to compete with the United States. On what ground woulld we be competing with them? For the annihilation of the fish. Through their up-to-date system of traps the United States have undoubtedly seriously menaced the salmon fisheries of the Pacific coast, and one has only to go down to the Fraser river and into Puget sound to realize the truth of that statement. Or he can go up to the southeastern Alaskan waters and find that Mr. O'Malley, the director of fisheries for the United States, has reduced the traps for the year 1929, in the very area we are speaking of, by the number of sixty. On what grounds? Because of the fact that the escapement of salmon is not sufficient and the catches have depreciated.
The fourth argument offered was that the largest amount of fish caught in foreign countries was caught by means of traps. In the short time at my disposal, I could not find any further arguments.
Let me take the argument which was advanced by the fishermen-and I think these men are entitled to the courtesy of a fair hearing because we are considering something greater than the mere scientific, expeditious method of capturing fish. The fishermen argued that many of them would be put out of employment. They proved that statement, and Judge Ellis admitted that the fishermen had proved their case. In his report Judge Ellis said that the fishermen had convinced him that the traps would reduce the number of fish they would catch and eliminate to some extent the number of men engaged in the fishing business, and the cannens admitted that that was true and that the number eliminated would depend upon the number of traps which were put into the water.
I find that there is no right or power vested in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to grant say three or four licenses at Wales island or Pearse channel and to refuse licenses to others in the same area. He cannot grant to some and refuse to others. What will be the result? According to the canners themselves the result will be that by the installation of traps they will be able to obtain a higher grade of fish and sell at a higher price. Can anyone argue that other canners in the same area will stand idly by and allow two or three of their number to reap the reward; that they will be content to take the lower grade of fish which they say are caught by the gill netters, the trollers and seiners? That is absolutely ridiculous. These traps will not only throw two or three hundred fishermen out of employment, but a living will be taken away from their wives and children.
Fish Traps-Mr. Brady

In this large district No. 2, there are 1,421 fishermen engaged in the industry, with three hundred more trawlers. These men buy their supplies from the various merchants in Prince Rupert and they contribute a large sum of money annually to the upbuilding of that town. They have a capital of $1,500,000 invested in boats. AM these matters should be considered, but, to my mind, the main one was not mentioned in the report.
I approach the discussion of this question with as open a mind as any man could have in order to investigate a question concerning which I was some time ago not fully informed. I agree that the trap is a scientific instrument for the catching of fish. It is deadly in its power; it is placed in the very path of the fish as they go to spawn and there is no hope of escape. The gill netter, the troller and the seiner must follow the tide hither and thither, and the fish have a sporting chance of escape as they go to the spawning grounds. The Americans are decimating and depleting their own waters, and it ill becomes us to put into operation a system so deadly in its effects and so dire in its results, one which destroys God's food to the people who for all times and for all ages have depended upon the food of the sea. It may seem sentimental for me to speak like this, but I have only to take you back, Mr. Speaker, to the days of Christ himself, when He, the representative of the poor, having no money with which to pay tribute to Caesar, ordered that a fish be caught, and in its mouth was found the coin that paid the tribute to the Roman emperor. This question is not one that we, as a people capable of understanding, can treat with light disdain and at the same time be true to the great heritage which is ours. Therefore I honestly believe that in putting those traps into those waters, we are doing something which will deprive future generations of the food that God Almighty Himself placed in the waters, believing that those fish would be the food of the common people for all time.
I do not see that the report of Judge Ellis, as I have read it, is based upon convincing arguments. Therefore, without delaying the house further, I ask that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries consider carefully the arguments advanced on both sides. He has found all the citizens of Prince Rupert opposed to those traps; the city council passed strong resolutions against them. Nine different associations of salmon trollers and fishers have asked him not to put those traps into effect. I know the minister believes that if he had those traps there, he would be better able to tag the fish and to follow their migration to the waters in order to ascertain whether they go into

Alaskan or British Columbia waters. But that is a minor question in the presence of a major one, which is this: I am here this evening endeavouring to represent to parliament the views of the people of British Columbia as a whole, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would be well advised, before putting into operation the recommendations of this commission, to ponder its report more carefully and at greater length, so that at least we may be assured that no injustice will be done to the people in No. 2 district and that there will be no depletion of the fish supply which is so valuable to the people of those parts of British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the indulgence of the house for a few moments while I refer to this subject. I regret that it comes up at this time, as in committee it might have been disposed of with a few questions to which, no doubt, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) would have been able to supply the answers. The traps in question are a subject of long standing, going back, I think, as far as three or four years. I find in the file a copy of a letter dated September 10, 1926, from the department to the company concerned, in which the department promised an investigation with a view of ascertaining what damage, if any, was done, and what obligation there might be on the part of the government on account of promises made, which the company interested claimed they had acted upon. In going through the file I find there does not appear to be any other correspondence of record until this royal commission comes up. In this regard I think a fair criticism of the Department of Marine and Fisheries is the fact that so much of their business is carried on apparently by personal negotiation and so little of it is a matter of record that it is very difficult for anyone to follow the proceedings in continuity. It is not necessary for me to point out to the house that in international negotiations in the past this failure to put our understandings on record has led, I believe, to some repudiations which were not pleasant. I am sure that in our negotiations here as well as with our neighbours to the south, the department will keep out of trouble, and the members of the house will be able to follow the proceedings with a great deal more clarity if they are all properly on record and not left to verbal understanding.
It would appear that in the early stages of this trap controversy on our northern boundary, the claim for damages was presumably made and the investigation then promised

Fish Tra-ps-Mr. McRae
apparently had that in view. This matter would have 'been much better dealt with had that now been the issue and had the government seen fit to order an investigation on the basis of whether we were responsible financially or morally in connection with the establishment of these traps some three of four years ago, instead of bringing up the old question of the establishment of traps.
It is unnecessary for me to go over this question again. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (;Mr. Neill) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) have dealt with it at length, and there is little I can add except to say that I thoroughly concur with them in their presentation of the situation.
A great deal of trouble would have been saved had the matter -been dealt with on the basis of compensation. I cannot think there is any politics mixed up in this at all, because it certainly would be very bad politics. I notice, however, in going through the file, that a letter was sent to Mr. Olaf Hanson on March 27 last advising him that a commission was appointed, but apparently he never replied; at least there is nothing on the file to show that he did.

speechtext:
The opponent of the hon.
member for Skeena in the next election. I can only say that if Olaf did not reply, it goes to show not only his great inexperience but that he has a great deal to learn in the political game, because even to a blind man it should be apparent that this would be ruinous to the chances of any candidate. I hope in the committee, in order to square Olaf, to show that he has'ordinary sagacity in matters of this kind, the hon. minister will be able to produce a letter from him telling the minister not to go ahead with this commission under any circumstances because to do so will mean the return of Jim Brady.
This problem as it manifests itself in the north is right on the border line between British Columbia and Alaska, and the situation is almost identical with that of Fraser river. I suggest to the minister that when he is redrafting the Fraser river sockeye treaty for next session, he include the Naas problem, because it is an international water. The satisfactory adjustment depends entirely upon our coming to an agreement with the United States, and I do not hesitate to say, as I said in committee the other day, that unless
something is done in connection with the Naas River, it will soon be as barren of fish as the Sahara. There will be no fish in it at all and nothing to trouble about. That would be a most regrettable condition, and I think that the proper way to deal with this matter is in an international way.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I was not going to refer to the question of traps exceipt to endorse the position taken by the two hon. members who have spoken. I do, however, want to take exception to one or two of the findings of the royal commission in the hope that in view of our united opposition the recommendation to establish traps will not be adopted. I see that the minister himself has a pretty fair idea of traps because, if my memory serves me aright, in speaking a few days ago of the haddock traps he said that they required few men. That is true of traps whether they be on the Pacific or the Atlantic coast. The report of Commissioner Ellis would indicate that there are now some 11,000 fishermen engaged in fishing on our coast. Last year, 1927-28, the total number of licenses granted to all kinds of people, red, white and yellow, was 14,819, and that, I would have hon. members understand, is for a very much depleted industry. If our fishing industry on the Pacific coast was built up to what the people of this country have a right to expect, there would be about 50,000 licenses issued a year, and that industry alone, built up on that basis of individual licenses as now issued, keeping away from traps, would support a population as great as that of Prince Edward Island.
