speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
I have only a few words to say in reply. From the observations made by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this matter, I can readily understand that there is a very strong opposition to the issuing of licenses for traps in the northern waters of British Columbia.
As has been stated, this is not a new question. It has been in the mind of the public for many, many years; in fact, licenses have been issued as far back as 1916. In that year two licenses were issued; in 1917, 5; in 1918, 6; in 1919, 7, and in 1920, 6.	The department has received
complaint against the issuing of these licenses, and the officers have been looking into that question with some care. I think, however, it would be unfair to conclude that the present government is the only one responsible for these traps. Indeed, in that respect, the record of the Liberal government can be compared favourably with that of previous administrations. Licenses were issued in 1925 on the understanding that the company should not be too sure that they would be renewed in 1926; in fact the licenses were not renewed in 1926 until after this government went out of power. After we went out of power, on July 23, 1926, licenses were issued to that company, the Canadian Fishing Company, by the then government, but on account of representations made on the 4th of August, 1926, a report was asked for, and the result was that on August 16, 1926, less than a month

after the licenses had been issued on July 23, they were cancelled by the present government.
As hon. gentlemen have pointed out, it is a complex and difficult question. The department felt that we should not renew the licenses and the matter has been under consideration in the meantime. After receiving representations from the fishermen and from the company concerned, it was considered advisable to have an investigation made by an independent organization, and it was thought that a judge would be sufficiently independent to take the evidence which might be given on both sides of the issue and carry on that investigation. I confess that, this report having come to the department at the end of the session when we were very busy, it has not been given by the officers of the department or by myself, owing to lack of time, a detailed study. I can only say at present that no one should conclude that because the commissioner recommends the licensing rf a certain number of these traps it is (he intention of the department and myself to follow his recommendation. I once more submit that a department or a minister is not bound to follow the recommendation of any commissioner who may have been appointed in order to provide the minister with better information and fuller detail on the question under consideration. In that case as in an3' others, the reasons given by the commissioner and his conclusions will be weighed in the light of experience, and I can assure the house that the interests of the fishermen will not be prejudiced, and nobody need be alarmed lest the matter be decided without proper consideration being given to the recommendations.
My hon. friend from North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) referred to the fact that the documents which I showed him were not very complete. As a matter of fact they are all we have. I know the matter has been discussed verbally with people from British Columbia by the officers of the department and myself. I should not like the impression to prevail that our files are not properly kept. They are kept in good order, and documents which should be on those files are to be found there. In fact the letter written by the Hon. Mr. Patenaude-he was Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries for a short while-in which he promised an investigation was not on the departmental files. It is on there today because that promise was used as an argument by the company asking that licenses be issued in their favour. When we asked

In former years I have dealt with this matter at some length and pointed out that as a commeicial proposition, peat fuel is not in the class of fuel that can be dealt with mechanically. There are about 4,000,000 people in Ireland and they consume about 8,000,000 tons of peat; that supply is obtained by peasants spading it out

in the spring months, stacking it up to dry and using it during the ensuing eleven or twelve months of the year. It is not a mechanical proposition at all but a domestic one. As the minister knows, the water content of peat is very high. In discussing this question on a former occasion the minister referred to the difficulty of drying peat in this country particularly in the summer months, because of the moisture in the air. Unfortunately that is true; there is much more moisture in the air in warm weather than is the case in cold weather. When the temperature is below zero there is no moisture in the air at all; it is completely dried out, but during the summer months the moisture content is very high and it is much higher on some days than on others. That affects the water absorbed by the peat just as a sponge absorbs water; the combined moisture cannot be abstracted by solar heat or anv other kind of heat. I believe the minister is aware of that fact; that is the great difficulty and it is one reason why peat has a very low fuel value.
There are three difficulties in connection with peat; ithe first is its low thermal value; the second is its bulk and the third is its friability and the difficulty of handling it without reducing it to powder. maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
I understand there has
been some misunderstanding with the people who have taken it over.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
We have
nothing to do with them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
Under what conditions
was the plant taken over?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
The coal was being purchased from the Western Dominion Collieries, and a large proportion of the money invested in those collieries was English money. Mr. Sutherland, who was in charge, has since died but the mine is still controlled by the same company. They have decided to erect a plant at Bienfait upon the premises occupied by the original experimental plant, erected by

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
the Lignite Utilization Board. We are not connected with She matter in any way except that they hope to come under the provisions of the domestic fuels act, while we do not believe that they can come within the provisions of that act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
I understand that that
plant was erected for the purpose of briquetting brown coal; is that the fact?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext: It is Canadian lignite; I do not know whether you would call it brown coal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext: Yes, it is the same thing. I do not see any possibility of their coming within the provisions of the coking act because briquetting and coking are two totally different operations and there is no connection between them. There has been a considerable amount of correspondence between the department and these people.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
It is very
difficult for me to see just how they can come under the provisions of the act, but they have a high temperature carbonization plant through which the coal is put before it is briquetted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FISH TRAPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA WATERS
speechtext:
Their idea is simply to
heat the coal to a temperature of four or five hundred degrees in order to make it plastic by liberating some of the oils and tarry substances in the hope that thereby they will then be enabled to briquette it. Whether that will actually work out in practice remains to be seen, but that is beside the question. If those people are prepared to spend their own money in making that experiment, I have no objection, and I do not think the minister will object.
